This subject focuses on contemporary Aboriginal Sydney as a means for exploring current and historical ideas about First Nations culture, Country, and community.

It uses a broadly transformative, social justice framework to challenge your assumptions and nurture your curiosity about First Nations ways of knowing and being, while exploring an urban context such as Sydney today.

Through incorporating a range of First Nations voices, it provides opportunities to identify how Indigenous Knowledges and perspectives intersect with your particular area of study and potential profession.

Delivered completely online, each week you will draw from pre-recorded lectures, television drama, online tutorials and scholarship by leading First Nations authors to critically analyse concepts such as identity, place and First Nations self-determination.

You will be introduced to important protocols essential to your professional practice, and the subject's two written assessments offer opportunities to reframe your thinking using a strength-based lens that recognises First Nations agency and the ongoing need for truth-telling and healing.
Through our criterion-focussed assessment, we will also provide you with rich feedback to encourage greater criticality and analysis in your essay writing and professional reflection.

Fieldwork Report (Report, 60%). This assessment requires you to undertake 2 to 3 semi-structured interviews with friends/family focusing upon the broad topic of 'oral health and hygiene'. Interviewees must be individuals with whom you are familiar and with whom you have an established relationship as we do not have ethical clearance to interview anyone else. The interviews will explore interviewees' behaviours, motivations, experiences, and understandings around this broad topic. This is an opportunity for you to explore and unpack a topic/area of everyday life which we all may to some extent 'take for granted' and not regularly discuss or share with others. Interviews should be between 15-20 minutes each. You can either take handwritten notes only during the interviews or also supplement such notes with a digital recording (so long as you have verbal consent of the interviewees). Upon completion of the interview, you will take 10 minutes to write notes to reflect upon the experience of the interview including reflection upon your own role in the process and what you consider went well/could be further strengthened/was a challenge (do please note that the longer you leave between completing the interview and undertaking this task, the less details and rich insights you are likely to remember). The semi-structured interviews need to be framed around questions that can help you explore the following areas: The interviewees' understandings of what oral hygiene/health constitutes; The regimes, practices and products used by the interviewees to maintain/improve oral hygiene/health (what they use and why they use them); The interviewees' motivations and expectations regarding their own oral hygiene/health and the oral hygiene/health of family/friends; The interviewees' perspectives and understandings around who is influential (significant others) regarding their oral hygiene/health behaviours and regimes and in what ways these significant others are influential. The 4 areas outlined above act as the overarching structure for your interview guide. However, your job is to compose 2-3 specific questions for each of the 4 areas above (8-12 questions in total). Remember, you'll also have to begin the interview by introducing yourself, the project (in very general but clear terms - do not explain or read out the details of the theme list/interview guide) and what is expected of them and you during this fieldwork experience. Keep in mind that many interviewees may never have participated in qualitative research or qualitative interviews before and do not necessarily assume they are familiar with what is involved and/or expected of them. To analyse your collected data you must undertake a basic Framework Approach analysis following the framework approach process and steps (as outlined in the Module 4.4). Do not attempt to use any other qualitative analysis approach in this assessment. Students will produce a report from the interview process and results. The report will follow a four heading structure (see Guidelines for Document Submission outlined below). Do please note: while addressing all four sections outlined below is essential to this assessment, please note the section dedicated to you providing critical reflection upon your fieldwork experience is of priority (and has been allocated largest wordcount and possible marks). Be careful to allocate sufficient word count to each section in accordance with the wordcount max provided.

Description: In this assessment, you will record a 5 - 6 minute video presentation reflecting on two peer-reviewed articles selected from a provided list on non-communicable disease (NCD) prevention and management. The aim is to link policy to lived experience and real-world responsibilities, showing how high-level strategies translate into everyday action and care.

Introductory regression analysis (Report, 25%). You will be given one dataset that you will need to read in to a software package (Stata). You will be asked to complete some basic descriptive analyses that develop the methods learnt in 090012 Fundamentals of Biostatistics as well as fitting linear and multiple linear regression models. You will be required to interpret the results of the analyses by writing simple, succinct summaries.

Statistical analysis of continuous and binary data (Report, 35%). You will be given one dataset to analyse. You will be given a number of short-answer questions that will require you to conduct linear or logistic regression analyses as appropriate, determine model fit, carry out appropriate diagnostics, and build appropriate statistical models. You will need to provide an interpretation of the models that can be read by someone not trained in biostatistics. You will need to justify your decisions about the statistical analyses and approaches that you have chosen. You will need to provide appropriate computer code, graphics, and summaries of your analyses in your answers.

Consulting report (Report, 40%). You will be given an epidemiological problem from a client (e.g. a public health or clinical researcher) and a dataset that you will need to analyse. The analysis will involve time-to-event data. The client, who is not trained in biostatistics, has requested that you provide her with an easily understood statistical report with a separate technical appendix. You have been asked to address the following in your report: Methods: you will need to describe and justify the methods you have chosen for analysis, your approach to model building, and any regression diagnostics and checks of model fit that you have undertaken. Results: you will need to summarise the results of your analyses, paying particular attention to providing a clearly written interpretation of your final regression model that can be understood by someone not trained in biostatistics. Strengths and limitations: You will need to discuss any strengths and limitations of your approach and of the regression model. You will need to provide appropriate computer code, graphics, and summaries of your analyses in the technical appendix.

What's the problem? (Essay, 25%, Individual). STEP 1 : Choose one of the following health-related innovations, which have been presented as solutions to particular problems in health: Activity-tracking apps (and associated wearable devices) - e.g. Fitbits, Apple Watch, etc. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based chatbots for digital mental health STEP 2 : Research the policies, peer-reviewed academic literature, and (credible) news media around these innovations, to critically analyse how these innovations have been developed, by whom, and to identify what assumptions they include, about the problem/s that they are designed to solve. Drawing on your research, answer the following 7 questions in a short answer essay format. You can refer to Australian and international examples in your answers. What is the 'problem' that is this innovation is represented as addressing? There may be multiple problems, if so, mention them all, but pick one to discuss in the rest of your report. What assumptions are made about the problem? (E.g. how the problem has come about, whose behaviour needs to change, what the barriers to solving the problem have been in the past, etc.) Who has been involved in developing, presenting and implementing this innovation, and who was not included? What sources did they draw on? (Private enterprise? Researchers? NGOs? Professional groups? Consumers? Advocacy groups?) Are there other ways of describing 'the problem', as described in your answer to question 2? For instance, are there other explanations for how the problem has come about? What are some of the possible consequences of implementing this innovation? (E.g. how might it impact on the way we talk about these issues, how does it portray people, how does it affect how people see themselves, how might it affect how people live their lives?) How has this innovation been implemented, disseminated (or marketed), and what are some alternative approaches to the problem? Reflecting on the research and analysis you have just completed, what is something you have learnt or reconsidered about the innovation you have chosen? (150 words) IMPORTANT : Your submission should also include a brief introductory statement to tell the reader which innovation you are investigating. TIPS: These questions are based on the WPR framework by Carol Bacchi , introduced in Week 1. You should review that module for resources and activities to understand the rationale and intent of each of the questions. The questions should be incorporated as headings. Your responses to each of the questions should be supported by references to relevant policies, government or NGO reports, peer-reviewed academic literature, and, where appropriate, from credible news media (e.g. The Conversation).

A toolkit for human-centred design (Presentation, 30%, Individual). SCENARIO You are a consultant who has been invited to give a presentation to a group of senior managers at a health and/or social care organisation. This presentation is an opportunity to win a contract to: deliver a set of resources and a program of training to upskill the organisation on desgining human-centred innovations. Review the project brief provided on Canvas for more details about the organisation and their particular needs. These methods/tools should assist innovators to: i) identify the needs and experiences of key users and stakeholders in the design process, and ii) prototype and test solutions within the context of the services that the organisation provides. [2-4 slides] A hypothetical example of how the service might use two of the HCD methods/tools identified to design an innovative solution, with the aim of "improving communication between consumers and service providers within the organisation" . A final slide with key takeaway messages.

An organisational guide to innovation (Report, 45%, Individual). SCENARIO The Head of Innovation at Uniting was happy with the presentation that you delivered in Assessment 2, and has engaged your consultancy to provide organisational training on human-centred design. As part of this contract, she has also asked for a guide on how to support human-centred design and design thinking within their organisation. In particular, she is interested in how the organisation can foster innovative thinking (mindsets) and systematically support the development and spread of innovations throughout the organisation. She is particularly interested in the challenge of engaging their clinical staff in innovation. To develop this guide, you should draw on what you have learnt in this subject, about approaches to fostering innovation within organisations, including: the organisational factors that support the development and spread of innovative practices in a complex health and social service organisation; and the regulatory frameworks, policies, standards and risks (e.g. privacy, confidentiality, equity, accountability/governance, patient safety) that need to be taken into consideration when designing and implementing innovations in that particular organisation. TASK You should submit a 2000 word report, supported by the research literature, which should include the following sections: a) Introduction - to explain what innovation is; why innovation is important in health and social care and for Uniting in particular; why human-centred design is an important approach for innovation; and the purpose of this document. b) Workplace culture c) Leadership and governance d) Infrastructures of innovation e) Ethics, risks, regulations and standards f) A list of key recommendations TIPS We expect you to demonstrate an understanding of the concepts taught in this subject. Start with the course-provided readings when doing your research. The mention of organisational training in the scenario is just for background information, it is not part of this assessment.

Personal improvement project proposal (Report, 20%, Individual). Create a simple plan to take the first steps towards improving one aspect of your own life over the course of the following five weeks in this subject. To make this achievable, you should choose something that occurs regularly and frequently (e.g. daily) and is within your control to change, such as your own behaviour. (TIP: keep it simple and focused.) Examples in your personal life may be: to be more physically active, set aside time for self-care, get more sleep, change your diet, reduce alcohol consumption, etc. Examples in your professional life may be: to better manage your emails, to increase your study time, to leave work on time more frequently, etc. In this assessment, you should apply the principles learnt in Week 1 to put together a short proposal. Follow the instructions below on how to structure this proposal and what to include. 1. Answer the following questions, using the headings (those in bold) in your submission. You should consider the points below the headings when answering the questions. Write in first person, and support your points with the literature where you can. a. What is the problem about, and what might you be able to do about it? How would you describe the problem to someone else? What information do you have, to show that this is something that needs to be improved? Is there information available in the research literature about other people's experiences of this issue? b. What are some actions (interventions) you could feasibly trial to address this problem now? Why do you think they might help? What might prevent you from taking those actions? What might help? If you have tried to address this problem before, your reflections on that process would be highly relevant and useful here. Is there information in the research literature about what interventions have been trialled by others, and their enablers and barriers? Which of these interventions would you trial first, and why? c. How are you going to know that you have made an improvement? What outcome measure/s could you record to understand what the current situation is so that you will know if it has changed in the future (improvement)? Note: before you change anything, you should first record this data for a period of time, as a baseline measure. What measure/s could you record to keep track of the processes that affect your outcomes? What measure/s could you record to keep track of what other important aspects of your life might be impacted by your project? (These are known as balancing measures.) d. What might be a realistic improvement to aim for in five weeks? Can you find information in the research literature to help you to determine what can be achieved, realistically, in five weeks? e. What is your proposed aims statement? Present your aims statement here, based on your answers to the above questions. Refer to the aims statement activity in Module 1 for support. 2. Next, create a record-keeping and reflection journal (not to submit), where you will record the following information: your data (what you choose to measure) recorded at regular intervals throughout weeks 2 to 6 the interventions that you have actioned ongoing and regular reflections on your project any modifications you have made to your plan. This journal can be kept whatever way suits you best - digitally (e.g. a spreadsheet) or on paper. Your records in this journal will be necessary to complete assessments 2 and 3. You do not submit this journal.

In this subject, students will explore the key components and workings of healthcare systems, focusing on the Australian healthcare system.
The course will cover how health systems are built, how they change over time, and how they operate.
Students will gain the skills needed to lead and make a difference in the healthcare sector.
Key areas of study include: 1.
Structure and Function: Understanding the organization and roles within the Australian health and social care systems. 2.
Service Delivery: Learning how health and social services are provided and the challenges faced. 3.
Policy and Governance: Examining how policies and governance impact healthcare delivery and outcomes. 4.

Health Inequities: Investigating how the structure, policies, and delivery of health services contribute to unequal health outcomes for different groups, especially Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. 5.
Equity and Access: Reflecting on the barriers to and enablers of equitable access to health and social care. 6.

Intersectionality: Understanding how various social categories like age, disability, mental health, location, socioeconomic status, refugee status, and migrant status intersect to influence health outcomes.
By the end of the subject, students will be able to critically assess healthcare systems and suggest meaningful ways to address health inequities.

This subject is essential grounding for clinicians, managers and planners of health and social care services, who seek to improve the value of care, within the context of expectations of clinical and corporate governance, organisational performance and workplace change.
The subject examines each of the components of quality, risk, health outcomes and cost as they relate to high value health and social care.
The subject aims to build core skills in new thinking in care delivery by focusing on the way care is planned, organised, managed and delivered in relation to quality, risk, health outcomes and cost.

Utilising the Institute for Healthcare Improvement's Triple Aim framework and Porter's Value-based Health Care Framework as a starting point, students will develop a critical view on the organisation of health care, measurement and delivery of outcomes, from the patient and population perspective, as well as organisational accountability for cost and quality.

The subject focuses on current approaches to quality and safety, identifying and maximising value in healthcare, patient/client satisfaction, and commonly recognised issues with healthcare delivery systems, as well as different ways of organising and managing health care.

text: Policy briefing on obesity treatment options (Project, 50%, Individual). You are a policy analyst working in the health department of a State government. The Minister has decided to increase the funding available for treatments for obesity in their State's public hospitals, in response to Strategy 3.3 of the National Obesity Strategy 2022-2032 ( page 61 ) . As ever, resources are limited and the Minister will only provide funding for either a surgical treatment (e.g. bariatric surgery) or non-surgical medically-supervised treatment (e.g. very low-calorie diet with/without medication). The Minister is also considering whether, once funded and available to all, the treatment should be mandatory for severely obese patients before they can access other elective procedures in public hospitals (e.g. IVF, joint replacements). Write a policy briefing for the Minister to guide them in their decision-making. It should contain the following elements: Identify the impact of obesity on the population and health system that justifies public hospital funding for an obesity treatment. A policy analysis that compares surgical and non-surgical treatments on the basis of: Cost-effectiveness evidence Equity Feasibility Outlines the ethical considerations of making obesity treatment mandatory for access to other elective procedures Provides recommendations to the Minister to aide their decision-making Note: The decision to fund a surgical or medical treatment for obesity has been made. Do not consider lifestyle or preventative options in your response.

Human Resource Management: What is it? Where did it come from? And, where is it going?

Human Resource Planning: how does the labour market impact on the practice of HRM in organisations?

Employee Selection: How are employees 'usually' hired?

Evaluating HRM: What is the future of HRM?

text: Competing in the Marketplace (Individual) (Project, 30%). Part 1 This assessment task focuses on the current health of your company. To assess this health, marketing managers often employ the 5C framework, which describes the company, collaborators, customers, competitors and the overall climate in which the company operates. In this task, you will take stock of the 5Cs of your company and describe possible trajectories for them. You will identify the value that your company seeks to offer its customers and critically evaluate the 5Cs against this proposed value. You will consider how indigenous cultures and contexts manifest themselves in each of the 5Cs. Part 2 This assessment task focuses on identifying and evaluating the sources of competitive advantage for your company. To assess these sources, marketing managers often employ the VRIO framework, which evaluates whether particular resources or capabilities are valuable, rare, costly to imitate and organized to create value. In this task, you will focus on the resources and capabilities of your company as identified in assessment 1a and beyond (as for example discussed in module 2). You will pick one of the resources or capabilities which you deem most likely to create competitive advantage and evaluate this resource or capability according to the VRIO framework.

subject_name: Marketing in the Age of Technology
text: Developing a Marketing Strategy to Create Brand Value (Individual) (Report, 40%). This assessment task focuses on developing a marketing strategy to create brand value. Brand value is often one of the intangible sources of sustained competitive advantage and it requires long-term strategic thinking as it involves building associations in consumers' minds and stable relationships. In this task, students will develop a marketing strategy for the offering they considered in assignment1 Part 1 and 2. Based on the current context of their company (the 5Cs as identified in assignment 1 Part 1) the task is to propose several steps to make the brand a source of sustainable advantage (as discussed also in assignment 1 Part 2). Students will reflect on the implications of their proposed strategy for their company's Indigenous stakeholders.

Future Trends and Challenges
With the advent of climate change, health crises, and global pollution there is a global trend and need for responsible investing and sustainable finance practices.
Artificial Intelligence (AI) has tremendous potential to accelerate and industrialise evidence-based, data-driven sustainable finance, ESG-related decision making, and climate risk management.
Natural language processing (NLP) and spatial AI have become leading technologies in this area, as have simulations, digital twins, virtual worlds, and omniverse.

Asset managers, asset owners, banks, insurance companies, regulators, and central banks are increasingly applying ESG criteria as part of their analysis process to identify material risks and growth opportunities.
Developments in AI and machine learning have led to the creation of a new type of ESG data that do not necessarily rely on information provided by companies.

In this subject we review the use of AI in the ESG field: textual analysis to measure firms' incidents or verify the credibility of companies' concrete commitments, satellite and sensor data to analyse companies' environmental impact or estimate physical risk exposures, machine learning to fill missing corporate data (e.g., greenhouse gas emissions).
We discuss potential challenges, in terms of transparency, manipulation risks and costs associated with these new data and tools.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has revolutionised the investment profession, enabling investment managers to process vast amounts of data, identify patterns, and make informed decisions with unprecedented speed and accuracy.
The subject provides practical skills in leveraging AI techniques for investment decision-making and risk management in the modern financial markets.
Students will explore the intersection of AI and investment management, highlighting the transformative role of AI in enhancing investment strategies, risk analysis, and portfolio optimisation.

For instance, robo-advisors have gained popularity as automated investment platforms that utilise AI algorithms to provide personalised investment advice and portfolio management services to individual investors.
In quantitative trading, AI models analyse historical data to identify market inefficiencies and execute trades automatically, capitalising on short-term price discrepancies.
In this subject, students learn the principles, methodologies, and practical applications of AI in investment and risk management.

Through hands-on exercises and projects, students will apply these techniques to analyse financial market data, evaluate investment strategies, construct optimised portfolios, and quantify and manage various financial risks.

The course will also address the ethical considerations associated with the use of AI in investment and risk management, such as bias and fairness, interpretability of AI models, and the impact of algorithmic decision-making on market dynamics.

Algorithm Implementation and Journal Reflection (Project, 50%, Individual). The goal of this assignment is to develop your hands-on skills in performing learning from data, as well as further understanding of the practical technical details of the learning procedure. For this assignment, your program should perform one of two tasks: Option 1: Demonstrate your understanding of a specific machine learning model within the context of the learning theory framework introduced in the subject. Your program should be designed to explain and illustrate the principles and functioning of the chosen algorithm, highlighting its benefits, drawbacks, and appropriate use-cases. Option 2: Propose a learning-based system to solve a practical task. This task can be anything from predicting stock prices to identifying patterns in images or text. Your program should implement the learning system, demonstrating its ability to learn from data and make accurate/useful predictions or decisions. Remember, the focus here is not merely on the practical problem, but also why you believe a learning-based system is an appropriate solution to it, and how. In both cases, you should tie your work back to the concepts and frameworks we've discussed in class. This task is AI open. You are encouraged to employ AI assistance tools to accomplish this task. You are required to explain the process of accomplishing the goal of the task. Therefore, the assessment of the submission will be according to the following procedure. Submission The assignment should be completed in three parts: a computer program implementing a machine learning model, an implementation memo and a presentation. The program and the memo will be submitted to fulfil this task: Computer program of a machine learning model. The implementation should be ready to run on a cloud-based platform. Project Implementation Journal. This is a detailed account of the entire journey of the project, including the design, implementation, log and reflection. Please pay special attention to account how you have utilised AI-tools to assist in each step. The submissions will be assessed during an interactive peer-review process according to the following criteria . The procedure of running the process is specified in Assessment Task 3 (where the aforementioned presentation is used). Important criteria: "Completeness of Explanation": 1) you are able to independently explain a concept is considered as full understanding. OR 2) you are able to show evidence in the memo report that an issue has been queried with an AI-assistance, and the result has been critically studied is also considered as FULL understanding. "Linking Machine Learning Concepts with Program Components": you should be prepared to illustrate, upon request, how certain theoretical concepts have been designed, implemented, or reflected within your program. This demonstration should ideally be reflected within your memo report, drawing clear connections between machine learning theories and the practical aspects of your project. "Functional": the program runs without exception in anticipated cases. For edge cases, e.g. size of data being large for the complexity of the program, the issue has been expected and explained. More details will be released in specification documents on Canvas site.

Serious Games Studio Project (Project, 100%, Group, individually assessed). You will work in a team to design, build, and evaluate your own serious game across the whole semester. Everything connects into one continuous project that develops step by step, like a real game studio. You will start by coming up with a game idea that addresses a real-world issue such as health, education, wellbeing, or the environment. Early on, you will also reflect on how your design would need to change if you were working with an Indigenous Australian community, using established cultural and intellectual property protocols discussed in class. From there, you will develop a full research and design proposal. This becomes your project roadmap and includes your Game Design Document, background research, and a plan for how you will evaluate whether your game actually works as intended. Next, you will build a small proof-of-concept prototype. This is not about polish, it is about testing whether your core idea works in practice and learning from it early. After that, you will expand and refine your game into a more complete playable prototype, using feedback and testing to improve your design and systems. Finally, you will submit your finished prototype along with a short research report that explains what you built, how it evolved, how you tested it, and what you learned through the process. This subject explores the evolving role of the Australian computing industry, emphasising its shift towards leveraging computers for relationship maintenance, knowledge management, and innovation to gain competitive advantage.

You'll examine the industry's global context, the value of IT in business, and the implications of e-commerce, customer relationship management, user modelling, outsourcing, offshoring, and legal issues in the digital economy.
The subject also addresses organising business information, focusing on informal flows within organisations, and examines various work relationships, team formation, and management processes.
Practical skills include using portals and other tools for customer loyalty and outsourcing collaborations.

Journal Assignment (Journal, 20%, Individual). To develop students' sensitivities and perceptions about how people use technology in their everyday activities and the ability to articulate various issues around the design and use of technology from the perspective of its usability and usefulness. Students will work individually to produce three journal entries describing and critiquing real-world digital systems in terms of their design and use, that are relevant to the interests of the subject. While students are provided with the actual digital systems they have to write about for entries #1 and #2, they will have to actively seek out their own example for entry #3. For these journal entries, students have to observe and document people's interactions with the systems as well as apply their understanding of various design/usability concepts, theories and principles to analyse and critique the experience people have during these interactions. These may include poorly designed systems that do not support the activity they are used for, as well as systems that work well within their situation of use. Ongoing and formative feedback on journal entries #1 and #2 will support students to produce good work. A more detailed assessment brief for each journal entry will be provided on Canvas.

This is an open-book practical; books, websites, lecture and tutorial notes, and other materials can be used in the practical. Students will also design / draw / plan / sketch an interactive system. Students will be provided with all necessary information about this assessment via Canvas and during class time in Week 9.

Programming Exercises (Laboratory/practical, 30%, Individual). Individual work on lab exercises. The weekly lab exercises are designed to instruct students on fundamental game development techniques. Exercises are purposefully structured to require knowledge on topics that are not directly covered in the lectures, which in turn requires students to identify their own knowledge gaps and seek new sources of learning to complete development tasks. This promotes students to be proactive in their own learning and establish them as life-long learners in the constantly evolving game development industry.

Classic Game Recreation - Getting Started (Project, 20%, Individual). This assessment requires students to apply what they have learned to recreate a classic 2D game, drawn from the early eras of the games industry. At this stage, the project will need to have the scene for a single level set up, visual assets and animations created, audio files included and basic player movement functionality implemented. This will be a re-skinned game, meaning that all visual assets (sprites and animations) must be made by the student and audio files will need to be sourced from royalty-free providers, such that the game operates in the same way as the original while looking and sounding distinctly different to the original. Additional assessment details and marking rubric will be provided on Canvas.

Classic Game Recreation - Enhancing and Innovating (Project, 35%, Individual). This assessment extends upon Assessment 3 by requiring students to produce two scenes in their recreated game. The first scene is a full re-creation of the classic game in a manner that aligns with specified design constraints mentioned in the assessment specification document. This demonstrates the student's ability to interpret an existing game experience and re-develop it from scratch. While lower grade bands are achievable through knowledge and skills presented in the lectures, higher grade bands will require students to carefully plan solutions to previously unseen problems and be proactive in their learning to implement these. The second scene of the game will contain the student's own innovative twist to the core game mechanics and player experience, which exposes students to a design and development cycle of original content. Students are encouraged to push the boundaries of their skill in this second scene and seek new knowledge in order to implement their novel gameplay design. Additional assessment details and marking rubric will provided on Canvas.

Design Assignment (Project, 50%, Group, group and individually assessed). To provide students with opportunities to practise a Human-Centred Design methodology to focus on designing to support User Experience through combining user research, design and evaluation activities including theory, exploratory and experimental studies, prototyping and evaluation. Students will work individually and in teams of 4-5 to develop the interaction design for a system that supports good user experience . The project and the problem have been designed to provide opportunities to practise a human-centred design methodology in user experience design by combining user research, design ideation, prototyping methods and evaluation activities. Through this, students will develop personas, user stories, ideation, prototypes of the systems and evaluation of these prototypes in real life situations to refine the design of the system. Exercises during tutorials will provide students with opportunities to familiarise themselves with the various user experience techniques and tools used in this assignment. This games subject trains you to be an engineer of entertainment, teaching you the essential theoretical concepts and practical methodologies for game design.

Classic Game Recreation - Getting Started (Project, 20%, Individual). This assessment requires students to apply what they have learned to recreate a classic 2D game, drawn from the early eras of the games industry. At this stage, the project will need to have the scene for a single level set up, visual assets and animations created, audio files included and basic player movement functionality implemented. This will be a re-skinned game, meaning that all visual assets (sprites and animations) must be made by the student and audio files will need to be sourced from royalty-free providers, such that the game operates in the same way as the original while looking and sounding distinctly different to the original. Additional assessment details and marking rubric will be provided on Canvas.

Classic Game Recreation - Enhancing and Innovating (Project, 35%, Individual). This assessment extends upon Assessment 3 by requiring students to produce two scenes in their recreated game. The first scene is a full re-creation of the classic game in a manner that aligns with specified design constraints mentioned in the assessment specification document. This demonstrates the student's ability to interpret an existing game experience and re-develop it from scratch. While lower grade bands are achievable through knowledge and skills presented in the lectures, higher grade bands will require students to carefully plan solutions to previously unseen problems and be proactive in their learning to implement these. The second scene of the game will contain the student's own innovative twist to the core game mechanics and player experience, which exposes students to a design and development cycle of original content. Students are encouraged to push the boundaries of their skill in this second scene and seek new knowledge in order to implement their novel gameplay design. Additional assessment details and marking rubric will provided on Canvas.

Project Implementation Journal. This is a detailed account of the entire journey of the project, including the design, implementation, log and reflection. Please pay special attention to account how you have utilised AI-tools to assist in each step. T he submissions will be assessed during an interactive peer-review process according to the following criteria. Module 1: Problem Space This first module aims at the definition and the consequent analysis of problems characterized by some softness in complex environments
It will provide the theoretical background and practical tools to properly specify your case study and the issues associated
According to the process proposed, first of all, the context of the problem will be constructed by identifying the key stakeholders and the main relationships existing among them
A small research will provide information and insight as a consolidation
Then, stakeholder analysis will be performed by adopting tools (e.g. empathy maps and journey maps) which facilitate an analysis of the target scenario from multiple perspectives
Finally, issues and problems related to the different stakeholders will be identified
Module 2: Decision Space This module is the natural continuation of the previous and focuses on the formulation of a Joint Value Proposition (JVP) as a response to a problem previously identified
A JVP has to provide a clear value for stakeholder(s) and has to be formulated according to a SMART approach, meaning it has to be specific, measurable, assignable, realistic and time-related
Each student will define a JVP in the context of the problem space defined in the previous phase
Module 3: Solution Space This module focuses on a further development of the Joint Value Proposition which is described more in detail at a conceptual level
Such a conceptualization is related to the technology adopted and to the business (according to the Osterwalder's model), as well as it is materialized in a simple visual prototype

Honours Thesis (Thesis, 90%, Individual). Your Honours thesis will be a written record of your work on your Honours project during one academic year. It should be set in the context of the existing literature and theory relating to your thesis topic. Within the document, you should seek to explain or resolve a particular problem or several issues through your knowledge and skills in the mathematical sciences. This may be through the development of novel mathematical theory, may be new applications of existing theory, or may be an in-depth discussion and review of the literature of an advanced field of the mathematical sciences. If you have novel findings, whether in terms of the development of new mathematical theory or of a new application for existing results, the importance of these in the wider field should be noted and critically assessed. If your thesis is an exploration of the existing knowledge of an advanced field of study, you should provide a detailed discussion of the importance of the key theory and results, identifying some of the likely directions of future development in the research area. You are encouraged to use citations of other published work for methods and existing theory used in your project that are well known and well accepted within their field of study. Citations should be made according to the style format of an appropriate journal (usually either sequential numbering or as "surname (year)") within the main text. An accompanying References list should be included at the back of the thesis, before any appendices. Where large amounts of data or computer code are included in a thesis, these should be placed in electronic appendices, and not in the main body of the thesis. These appendices need only be included in the electronic submission of your Thesis, and not in the hard copies. The tone and clarity in the writing should be equal to that of published journal papers or commercial consultancy reports.

This subject offers a comprehensive and rigorous exposition to the theory and practice of financial risk measurement and management.

Conceptualise, design, plan and implement a data analytics project. (C.1)
Choose appropriate data analytics methods to achieve outcomes, apply them and evaluate their efficacy. (D.1)
Communicate the results of the data analytics investigation verbally and in written form at a level appropriate for a business audience. (E.1)
Contribute effectively in a data analytics team to achieve the desired outcomes. (E.1)

Plan and proposal (Report, 20%, Group, group and individually assessed). Based on the data mining problem and the group that you have formed, this task involves describing your group, the role of each team member, your proposal for solving the data mining problem and your plan for solving it. Assignments will be assessed based on the quality and plausibility of the proposal and plan and the completeness of team roles.

Mid-project update and presentation (Report, 30%, Group, group and individually assessed). In this assignment you will give a progress report on your work in the project to the client. Your group will describe the results of your data exploration and give initial findings as well as an updated project plan. This will involve a report as well as a short formal presentation to the client. Assignments will be assessed based on depth of data exploration, quality of understanding of the data mining problem as expressed through the initial findings and the understandability, professionalism and depth of the client presentation.

Final project and presentation (Project, 50%, Group, group and individually assessed). Your group will deliver a report to the client describing the results of the data analytics investigation. Your group will give a formal presentation describing the project and results to an executive panel from the client organisation (think of it as the company board).

In this subject students will apply Data Analytics Methodologies (CRISP-DM, SEMMA), Data Analytics Project Management (resource allocation, working in teams, planning, running meetings), use their skills for Data Interpretation and Communication of Results.
This subject culminates your data analytics skills through a team-based project that tackles real-world problems in academia or industry.
You'll manage investigations, document progress, and communicate findings.
The project encompasses data generation, processing, modelling, analysis, and result interpretation.
With an academic mentor's support, your performance is evaluated through written reports and an oral presentation, meeting academic and industry standards.
Demonstrate knowledge of human-centred design methods. (D.1)
Demonstrate an ability to plan, design and carry out small user research projects. (C.1)
Develop an analysis of the findings from user research suitable for use in professional projects. (B.1)
Explain results and outcomes to others in their cohort and to broader audiences through paper writing, poster and video presentations. (E.1)
Apply positive and respectful ethical practices, such as the AIATSIS Code and NHMRC's ethical code for researchers. (A.1, B.1)

Quiz on subject (Quiz/test, 10%, Individual). To provide students with an awareness of human-centred research methods as taught in this subject. Students are quizzed on their understanding of the subject matter, the way the subject itself is set up, and their responsibilities as ethical and people-focused researchers.

Poster on interviews (Report, 30%, Group, individually assessed). To provide students with the opportunity to put into practice and further develop skills in human-centred research. This includes literature research, developing relevant questions, performing interviews, qualitative data analysis, and communication of findings. The assignment requires students to work in groups of 3 or 4. They study and develop a research proposal, followed by contacting potential participants and performing in-depth interviews. Afterwards, students are encouraged to learn substantial methods for the analysis of data and its reporting. Online tutorials and class meetings give students the opportunity to receive guidance and feedback on their progress. SPARK will be used to answer questions about groupwork after submission.

Short report on probe design (Report, 10%, Individual). To provide students with the opportunity to put into practice and further develop skills in human-centered research. Following the direction set out in task 2, this task approaches similar research questions with another qualitative research tool, namely probes. Students will learn its application and analysis, and communication of findings. The assignment requires students to independently design and develop a probe kit, explain the research goal of the kit and how each of the probe kit elements contribute to reaching this goal. Visual material, such as sketches or photos should be included of the draft probe design. A draft positive and respectful informed consent form needs to be attached. A description should be added of the participant the student has invited to participate in their research, without revealing their identity. Online tutorials and class meetings give students the opportunity to receive guidance and feedback on their progress.

Presentation of analysis, short paper and video on probe study (Combination, 50%, Individual). To provide students with the opportunity to put into practice and further develop skills in human-centered research. Following the direction set out in Assessment Task 2 (group work), this task approaches similar research questions with another qualitative research method, namely probes. Students will learn its application and analysis, and communication of findings. The assignment requires students to individually study and develop a research proposal, followed by contacting a participant and asking them some questions (intro interview), then handing them a self-made probe kit and after pick-up performing an in-depth face-to-face interview (exit interview). In the last tutorial before the Assessment Task 4 submission deadline each student will be required to present the outcome of their thematic analysis in-class. This is a compulsory item to be able to get marks for Assessment Task 4. Compared to Assessment Task 2, this individual task puts more emphasis on the quality of writing a paper and dissemination of findings in an academic way. Due to the visual and physical nature of the probes method, a video deliverable enables students to communicate that part of their work effectively. Students need to demonstrate awareness and implementation of positive and respectful ethical practices. This includes applying the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander (AIATSIS) Code of Ethics when working with and for Indigenous Australians; demonstrating that they have gained approval of free, prior, and informed consent; and attaching a completed ethics form.
Throughout the session students will become familiar with the following topics:
Interviewing
Probes
Ethics in user research
Recruiting and engaging with participants
Analysis of qualitative research data
Reporting and communication of research findings, both in written and visual material
This subject focuses on making people the core of the interaction design process through human-centred design methods, with particular attention to the interviewing and probes methods.

Interviewing gathers direct information and adapts flexibly across the design process, while probes, using tailored props, require more setup but aim to inspire creative insights and prepare participants for a follow-up interview.
You'll learn both methods, applying them step-by-step to real participants, guided by a brief and with readings and examples to tailor your approach.
You must recruit at least three strangers (people you do not know and who are not familiar with the subject) for interviews and one stranger for the probe study.
Understand advanced concepts in games programming and conduct self-directed learning to explore such topics in-depth. (D.1)
Iteratively design and develop technical demonstrations that combine numerous forms of fundamental and advanced game development techniques. (C.1)
Collaborate with group members to share knowledge of advanced game development topics, resulting in the design of unified user experience. (E.1)
Abstract and communicate the intent, benefits, and complexities of an advanced game or tool design to a wider audience of peers. (E.1)
Critically analyse the prototypes of others and provide professional and constructive feedback. (E.1)

Weekly Lab Activities (Exercises, 30%, Individual). Become familiar with the core concepts and algorithms presented in the lecturer and establish a baseline prototype to develop further through the other assessments. Lab activities will be provided on Canvas for students to work through each week. These will be scaffolded such that clear instruction are provided to achieve a lower grade bracket, while higher grade brackets will require students to investigate and self-learn to design and develop a solution.

Create an Unreal Engine Tutorial (Project, 20%, Individual). Explore the Unreal Engine further by choosing from a wide selection of engine features, self-studying that feature, and creating tutorial to teach it to other students. The Unreal Engine has a vast array of advanced features, from lighting, to animation, special effects, world builders, pre-built behaviour trees, and substantial code architectures. In this assessment, students will have four sub-tasks in order to explore these further: Choose one of these features and explore it in depth. This can be a system that is interacted with through the Unreal UI (e.g. world building), one that is through Blueprints (e.g material shaders), one that is through code (e.g. the Gameplay Ability System), or one that requires a mixture of these. Create a written tutorial in the style of the lab activities from Assessment 1. This activity should scale well, presenting foundational knowledge at the beginning and a reasonable challenge by the end. After submission, students will be given tutorial activities made by other students and be required to complete them and provide an anonymous peer review along with their completed project files. Each tutorial's creator will then need to verify and mark the completed tutorials submitted by other students.

Artificial Intelligence and Procedural Content Generation Prototype (Project, 25%, Group, individually assessed). Demonstrate a deeper understanding of artificial intelligence and procedural content generation in games, beyond that of the lectures and lab activities, and communicate this knowledge with others. Work in groups of two to establish a unique prototype that will be built upon in Assessment 3 and Assessment 4. This prototype should be an interactive technical demonstration, highlighting the challenges in coding advanced systems in game-like virtual environments, rather than being a refined game design. Start this unique prototype by creating one advanced system per group member. Each group member may choose to design and build either an artificial intelligence or procedural content generation system. This may extend upon the existing system created through the lab activities or may be entirely new. This prototype will be extended in Assessment 4 to include other features and combine the two systems. Therefore, the two systems should be designed to complement and work well together (while still being two distinctive contributions) and be designed with the requirements of Assessment 4 in mind. The Assessment 3 prototype does not need to produce a polished and engaging build. Instead, you will create a short video of your work to demonstrate the key features of the prototype's design, code and its execution and communicate these to staff and other students.

Final Multiplayer Prototype (Project, 25%, Group, group and individually assessed). Demonstrate advanced knowledge of C++ programming in the Unreal Engine by producing a substantial game-based technical demonstration by incorporating networked multiplayer techniques into the existing artificial intelligence and procedural content generation systems created in Assessment 3. Finalise your group's technical demonstration by building upon Assessment 3 and the lab activities to incorporate networked multiplayer and your knowledge from Assessment 2 into your prototype. The project should now resemble a complex, unified prototype that creatively incorporates multiple advanced topics into a playable interactive technical demonstration. This prototype should be refined in its technical implantation, visual presentation, and user interaction, such that it is ready to be used in future employment portfolios.
Topics covered in the lecture and encouraged for further exploration through the assessment include (but are not limited to):
An introduction to the Unreal Engine
Strategic game-playing artificial intelligence
Networked multiplayer
Procedural content generation and dynamic difficulty adjustment
Multithreading in games
This developing level subject dives into the advanced games topics of artificial intelligence, procedural content generation, and networked multiplayer.
You will learn these topics by utilising the industry-standard game engine, Unreal Engine 5, and the C++ programming language.

You will learn skills and concepts through assessed weekly lab modules that will teach you skills and algorithms that are transferable between game development environments and that can generalise across many aspects of games development.

You will further develop your understanding of these topics and combine them in a session-long group project that will culminate in a novel game or tool prototype that enhances your portfolio and prepares you for significant contributions to third-year capstone projects.
The subject's development was supported by the 2019 Epic MegaGrants scheme.

This subject introduces the fundamentals of modern software development, more specifically, website development.
You will learn traditional and agile software development principles, methods, tools, and techniques, and explore current trends and challenges in software development.
You will also learn how to design, develop, and evaluate software that implements commercially realistic but manageably small requirements.
Teaching is delivered through pre-recorded lectures and hands-on workshops.
In your weekly workshops and assessment tasks, you will be given assignments to modify or extend existing software features or functions and, at times, to create new ones.
You will be encouraged to practice peer learning and collaboration, but ultimately, you must complete your tasks independently.
By successfully completing this subject, you will experience, understand the importance of, and be able to apply sound professional practices in software development.

Building professional reputation and accessing the hidden job market

This subject teaches you how to apply for professional engineering or IT internships and how to learn on the job.
You'll develop your commercial awareness and document your professional growth, while developing your awareness of professional ethics, safety, and how to communicate with employers.
Through a blend of workshops and tutorials, you'll engage in active learning, preparing in advance with provided resources.
In four key workshops, you'll gain essential knowledge and collaborate with peers.
Additionally, four intensive tutorials offer a platform to review your peers' work and exchange perspectives on how to effectively obtain a professional position and meet the learning outcomes.

Explain key concepts and applications of AI techniques. (D.1)
Design solutions to implement AI techniques to solve simple real world problems. (C.1)

AI technique demos (Presentation, 40%, Group, individually assessed). Assess students' ability to articulate their understanding of artificial intelligence techniques used to solve simple practical problems based on examples provided in labs. In this assessment task, students will work in pairs to develop four AI technique demo videos. Detailed tasks and deliverables will be available in assessment task 1 specification in Canvas subject site.

AI Project (Project, 30%, Group, group and individually assessed). Assess a student's ability to work in a small group, collaboratively develop a showcase of applying some selected AI techniques to solve an interesting real-world problem and effectively present the outcomes of the project. In this assessment task, each group will develop an AI application showcase by applying selected AI techniques to solve an interesting real-world problem and present the outcomes. The deliverables consist of two parts. One part is group-based deliverables which include a solution program with detailed annotations, a brief report about the AI technique used and how it is evaluated, and a video to present the project, including the problem to solve, how chosen AI techniques are used to solve the problem and evaluation. This part will be marked as a group and take 25% of the subject mark. The other part is individual-based deliverable which is a reflection report including self-reflection on the learning journey to complete this assignment and peer-reviews of group members in the context of this project. This part will take 5% of the subject mark.

Answer questions about key concepts and simple applications of AI techniques during an open-book exam. This subject enhances your grasp of Artificial Intelligence (AI), covering learning, natural language processing, computer vision, search, knowledge representation, and reasoning.
With lectures and practical labs focused on specific AI techniques, you'll learn to select appropriate models and algorithms for tasks and apply AI methods in simple applications.

You will be assessed by a knowledge test, a set of mini-AI application examples and a group project addressing a real-world problem using AI technique, reflecting your ability for exemplifying AI applications and designing AI solutions in practical scenarios.

Industry and Society Understanding and Analysis (Report, 20%, Individual). To understand the current industry and society needs with respect to NLP-related jobs and skills. This is an individual assessment where each student needs to search current job advertisements related to NLP, and analyse the skills needed for the jobs. Draft answers to questions provided answering questions about key learning from your internship experiences. Submit your Learning Plan to your peer review group by the due date 1b) Go to your Peer Review Group in Canvas and review your peers' work to give feedback in the first tutorial. 1c) Write a paragraph summarising the feedback you have received from your peers in tutorial 1 and include any decisions you have made about how you intend to change your work. Note: Marks for this assessment task will only be awarded to students who have uploaded their own work, reviewed peers' work, provided verbal feedback in their timetabled tutorial, and lodged a summary of the feedback they have received by the due dates designated in the Program section of this subject outline. As outlined in the Late Penalty clause c) section of this Subject Outline, students who fail to meet all requirements of the assessment including attendance at the tutorial will not pass Assessment Task 1. These are essential components of Course Intended Learning Outcomes E.2 & F.1.

Critical review of peers' professional practice portfolios (Exercises, 0%, Group, group and individually assessed). The critical review of peers' draft professional practice portfolios gives students the opportunity to give and receive feedback as a basis for reflection on how to improve their portfolios for final submission. This task has four parts: 2a) Students are required to continue reviewing an online professional practice portfolio that details some of their professional experiences. Their portfolio should: commence with a 'landing page' that includes an 'about me' section that is a brief autobiographical narrative of their journey to becoming an engineer and the key influences on their choice of specialisation (major)include their updated resume/curriculum vitae. include written reflection on the 2 topics designated in task 1 above (approximately 700 words on each topic). Each written reflection should refer to some theoretical literature (see subject resources in Canvas) using the APA referencing system. Include a cover letter addressing the selection criterion on page 15 of the 'Learning Guide.' Students are required to make the URL for their draft portfolios available to their Peer Review Group by the due date. 2b) Go to your Peer Review Group in Canvas to obtain the URLs of your peers' portfolios. Students review their peers' draft portfolios and make comments on Canvas. Students are required to provide verbal constructive critical feedback to their peer group in the tutorial. Following the tutorial, students should utilise the review feedback they have received to improve their portfolios for final submission. 2c) A paragraph summarising feedback received from their peers must be submitted after the tutorial to receive marks for this task. Note: A pass for this assessment task will only be awarded to students who have uploaded their own work, reviewed peers' work, provided verbal feedback in their timetabled tutorial, and submitted a summary of the feedback they have received from peers by the due dates designated in the Program section of this subject outline. As outlined in the Late Penalty clause c) section of this Subject Outline, students who fail to meet all requirements of the assessment including attendance at the tutorial will not pass Assessment Task 2. These are essential components of Course Intended Learning Outcomes E.2 & F.1.

Curated professional practice portfolio (Portfolio, 50%, Individual). The curated professional practice portfolio is designed to provide students with the opportunity to capture in writing a critical self-review and reflection of critical incidents in their work experience in relation to the Engineers Australia Stage 1 Professional and Personal Attributes. Utilising feedback provided by peers in the week 6 tutorial, students are required to finalise a curated professional practice portfolio demonstrating ability to: reflect on professional experience, conduct critical self-review and plan for professional development; articulate in writing the development of their professional identity to date and use these articulations to inform a response to selection criteria in a job advertisement. Students' finalised portfolios should demonstrate reader awareness by presenting information in a well organised and easy to navigate format with a professional level of language communication proficiency evidencing effective editing skills, and utilising APA referencing conventions where needed.

Interview (Presentation, 50%, Individual). Professional Persona : including name, discipline, and aspiration in the engineering industry and experience in the Mechanical Systems Design Studio 1. See Canvas for more details. 2. Four (4) artefacts : a. Artefact 1 (Design Critique) : This artefact should contain a detailed written description of the original design - how it works, its parts, sub-systems, how well it meets the design requirement and how you think it is assembled. Artefact 2 (Re-Design Requirements) : This artefact should provide a comprehensive list of issues that require re-design. This may be presented in a table format, including a comment/explanation of each issue and why re-design is required and a list of priorities. You may make personal suggestions for how re-design tasks can be grouped and allocated. Include any calculations, sketches, references that support your decisions. Submitted at end of Sprint 2/Week 6. c. Artefact 3 (Second-Generation Design) : Informed by the team's re-design priorities as a whole, in this artefact the individual should document their re-design work on a major mechanical component. Submitted at end of Sprint 3/Week 9 d. Artefact 4 (Presentation of the Second-Generation Design) : In this artefact the student should present an overall description of the final re-design as a whole and with specific focus on their part. Include images, video, calculations and sketches where they support your arguments. Consider whether or not your design changes were successful/necessary and what might you have done differently? Submitted at end of Sprint 4/Week 12 3. Engineering Design Journal (EDJ) : includes details on the individual learning journey, reflection and feedback from across the semester. Portfolio and Presentations (Portfolio, 100%, Group, individually assessed). To document the iterative learning process and artefacts that demonstrate the achievement of learning goals related to computing science. Students are expected to work in teams assuming the role of a professional colleague throughout the project phase. Although students work in teams, their submissions are assessed individually. The computing science portfolio and presentations are carefully designed and assigned as four components. Each component informs the next component so that tasks are expected to be completed in the order proposed to obtain optimal success in the studio. A performance level rubric is used to identify individual progress during the 12-week semester in view of students making individual improvements to their performance level based on continuous feedback and opportunities for personal reflection. The components include: Component 1: Project Initiative Groupwork: Group; Individually assessed Length: 1000 to 1500 words, reference is excluded. The intent of this component is to train the ability to construct a project team and initiate a project, with clearly defined topics and tasks, team responsibilities, and management strategies. Following the training of research essentials in Sprint 1, students are required to construct a project team with 4-5 members sharing similar interests and with complementary skillsets and conduct substantial research to define their research topics and problems. Each team must develop a project proposal with a clearly defined research topic and feasible methodologies, as well as functionated team responsibilities and a strategic plan of project management. Students are strongly encouraged to communicate with relevant academic researchers at UTS for topic-specified consultation and advice. The Project Initiative encompasses three deliverables: Project Proposal including a research topic, involved methodologies, and expected outcomes. Statement of Team Responsibilities including team roles and task allocations. Project Management Plan including project management strategies, risk analysis, and project timeline with milestones. Component 2: Project Progress Groupwork: Group; Individually assessed Length: 1000-2000 words, reference is excluded. The intent of this component is to train the ability to proceed a project with the implementation of essential research skills, e.g., introducing research topics, searching and collecting research literature, and implementing basic methodologies, and reflect a team's learning journey with evaluations. Following the training of academic writing in Sprint 2, each team is required to introduce their research topics with the appropriate use of critical thinking skills, propose a feasible search strategy and collect at least 3000 articles aligning with their topics, and start to implement bibliometric methodologies and tools to analyse the data with raw results. Students are strongly encouraged to communicate with relevant academic researchers at UTS for topic-specified consultation and advice. The Project Progress encompasses four deliverables: Introduction including the background information of the selected topic and the motivation of choosing this topic. Data Profile including search strategies and the descriptive statistics of the data. Raw Results including some results generated by involved methodologies and bibliometric tools, with a mixture of tables and figures. Project Management including the contributions of team members (linked with their responsibilities), the update of the project timeline with milestone achievements, and potential risks and challenges. References must follow the UTS APA referencing style, with an appropriate use of reference management tools. Component 3: Project Solution Groupwork : Group; Individually assessed Length : Deliverable 2: Project Portfolio (at least 3000 words). The intent of this component is to train the ability to develop a project solution with a multifaceted skillset of research essentials, academic writing, and success in research. Following the training of extensive skills for research success in Sprint 3, each team is required to develop a solution for their pre-defined topics, and deliver the results through a coherent and logical framework and with insightful discussion using critical thinking skills. The Project Solution encompasses two deliverables: Deliverable 1: Project Presentation Each team is required to give a presentation to report their solution to the class, around 20 minutes. The presentation must cover the following content: Introduction of the Research Topic Data Profile Analytical Results Critical Review Conclusions All team members are required to present a part of the project, particularly reflecting their own contributions. Deliverable 2: Project Portfolio Each team will report their project solutions in a Project Portfolio, including the following contents: Introduction Data Profile Analytical Results Critical Review Team Responsibilities and Evidence Conclusions The report must follow a coherent and logical framework and present results with an appropriate mixture of tables and figures. References must follow the UTS APA referencing style, with an appropriate use of reference management tools. Component 4: Reflection and Responsible Research Groupwork: Individually assessed Length: 1000-1500 words. The intent of this component is to train the ability to reflect on the progress of self-development and learning journey and development of the understanding of research ethics. Students are required to evaluate their activities in this subject with critical thinking skills and identify their gains and pains along with the entire journey of the subject. Students are required to discuss their understanding on research ethics and how they practiced responsible research in their individual assignments and teamwork. Students are also encouraged to propose a responsible research plan for their future career development in a research-based environment.

Project 2: Build your own network You will build your own network using Cisco switch and router. Your job is to initialise the switch and router, complete basic configurations in hosts, switch and router. You will demonstrate the network routing status and connectivity, and analyse the network traffic.

This subject introduces the principles and practice of modern computer networking through a top-down exploration of the Internet and the TCP/IP protocol suite.

Using Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach as the core text, students examine how networked applications communicate, how data is transported reliably and efficiently, how packets are routed across networks, and how link-layer technologies support end-to-end communication.
The subject combines conceptual understanding with practical experience.
Students will analyse live network traffic, develop client-server applications using socket programming, and configure Cisco networking equipment to design and build functional networks.
Through these activities, students will strengthen their ability to troubleshoot network behaviour, evaluate network services, and design efficient, reliable applications and network solutions.

By the end of the subject, students will have a solid foundation in Internet architecture, network protocols, and practical networking skills relevant to IT, software, data engineering, and cloud-connected systems.

For this assessment, each student will work on a real-world case involving email spamming using skills learning in this subject. The primary objective is to analyse the email dataset, extract meaningful features for spam activity, and identify spam emails. Using analytical tools and techniques such as regression models, Support Vector Machines (SVM), or deep learning methods. Students are required to submit a report including their methodology, analysis, and results. Students are also required to demonstrate their results onsite to the teaching staff.

Students are required to submit a report including their methodology, analysis, and results. Students are also required to demonstrate their results onsite to the teaching staff.
