An essay to conduct independent research on one of the latest system security topics. (Report, 30%, Individual). This assessment is for students to conduct independent research on one of the latest system security topics. Students will be required to follow the standard procedure to investigate research papers in the area of system security. Students must generate a proposal to address system security problems and present their ideas to their peers and the teaching staff in a 5-minute presentation. Students are required to submit a research essay of approximately 1500 words as well as present a 5-minute talk. This essay should consist of: a proper title and an abstract for a chosen topic description of the research problem and brief findings literature review and synthesis of findings using appropriate referencing

Demonstration and Validation (Practical test, 20%, Individual). This assessment verifies students' understanding of weekly workshop content through hands-on demonstration and Q&A. At the end of each workshop, students are required to present their completed practical tasks to the teaching staff, demonstrate the functionality or outcomes of their work, and respond to questions that assess their technical understanding and problem-solving process. This assessment ensures students can apply system security concepts in practice and can clearly explain the techniques, tools, and reasoning behind their solutions. Students will be assessed on: • successful completion and demonstration of workshop tasks • accuracy and clarity of explanations provided during Q&A • engagement with workshop activities and troubleshooting steps

Online Quiz (Quiz/test, 10%, Individual). This online quiz will assess student's appliance of system security, internal mechanisms and broad Information Technology knowledge related to computer system security. Students must demonstrate an ability to relate, justify, analyse and respond to questions around system security, technical vulnerabilities, technical remedies and cyberspace security and safety under examination conditions. It includes 2 in-workshop Canvas quizzes of 30 minutes each (complete during the scheduled workshop session), which consists of discussion and application type questions for case analysis and problem solving tasks. Students will respond to a set of questions including multiple choice and short answer questions during the quizzes.

A project to identify security vulnerabilities and propose technical solutions to rectify them. (Project, 40%, Group, individually assessed). This assessment task is for students to identify security vulnerabilities by various attacks and hardened systems. The students will be grouped into defensive and offensive teams. The offensive team has to choose a subset of the top ten vulnerabilities listed on OWASP project website, identify these vulnerabilities in systems nominated by the defensive team and document their findings. Defensive team students will be tested on their ability to harden the system. Both teams are required to verify experimental outcomes and to propose solutions to remedy the identified vulnerabilities. Students are required to submit a technical report of approximately 2500 words and demonstrate their results onsite to the teaching staff. This report should consist of: an overview of the chosen vulnerabilities description of technical findings and supporting evidence in screenshots analysis of technical findings discussion and justification of potential remedy actions based on findings.

Secure Programming and Vulnerability Assessment (Quiz/test, 20%, Individual). To practice secure programming skills (e.g., C/C++) and investigate and understand real-world security vulnerabilities. Students will need to understand the root causes of the vulnerabilities and classify them into the corresponding bug types. Through the practices in quizzes, students are required to inspect and understand example vulnerability code fragments. Students will be given a source code that contains vulnerabilities - and will need to identify what line they are in and what kind of vulnerability they are as part of your report. In the quiz - students will be given, multiple choice and short answer questions that inquire about security vulnerabilities in a source code case study. Quiz is individually assessed.

Source Code Representation for Software Analysis (Project, 20%, Individual). To demonstrate how compilers represent various real-world source code fragments as an appropriate representation for software security analysis as a foundation for building software security tools. Students will need to understand source code representation and basic concept of software analysis and testing, including the knowledge of compilers, intermediate representation of source code, and how to compile and represent various real-world source code fragments as an appropriate representation for software security analysis. To demonstrate this understanding, the student will be working on LLVM compiler and SVF code analysis framework to develop a graph traversal on code graphs. Students are required to submit well-documented code implementation they have developed to output the desired results.

Software Verification and Testing (Portfolio, 15%, Individual). To practice and apply software security analysis techniques and start building automated source code analysis tools based on the code representation (in Task 2) to automatically reason about a program's properties (e.g., control- and data-flows) or program execution states. In this task, students will apply source code analysis techniques to capture source code properties and verify the assertions embedded in the code. Students are required to submit well-documented code implementation they have developed to output the desired results.

Automatic Detection of Security Vulnerabilities (Project, 15%, Individual). To deliver and evaluate the effectiveness of the developed security analysis and testing tool (Task 3) in detecting and defending a range of vulnerabilities. In this task, the student will leverage and apply techniques to automatically perform assertion-based verification for code using static symbolic execution.

Vulnerabilities scanning, exploiting and penetration testing report. (Portfolio, 30%, Individual). To implement common computer security attacks, complete short exercises with common penetration testing software, and investigate common vulnerabilities and report on the results. In this task, the student will conduct penetration testing, including port scanning, session hijacking and password cracking. Students are required to submit a penetration testing report and a presentation video to demonstrate the results.

Critical Discussion and Inquiry Exercise: Exploring Given Topics (Exercises, 20%, Individual). To demonstrate the ability to engage in critical discussion, effectively communicate understanding, and express inquiry on given topics. This assessment task is intended to allow students to critically engage with the material covered in this subject throughout the session. Through pre-readings, collaborative discussions in the class, case studies, and reflections, students formulate their responses to questions designed to encourage reflexivity.

Data Storytelling Blog post (Essay, 10%, Individual). To critically discuss and reflect on Australian Indigenous knowledge systems and practices as examples of cultural information systems. Students are to write a data storytelling blog post that explore Australian "Indigenous knowledge systems and practices" as examples of cultural information systems. Students will explore and communicate how Indigenous knowledge can be conceptualised as cultural information systems, fostering an appreciation for the rich heritage and wisdom embedded in these traditions. This task aims to develop students' skills in data storytelling, critical analysis, and effective communication while encouraging a thoughtful exploration of cultural diversity and information systems in the context of Australian Indigenous communities.

Data Warehouse Design (Case study, 15%, Individual). To enhance database design skills, specifying Extract, Transform, Load (ETL) processes and emphasize the pivotal importance of data quality and consistency throughout the design of a data warehouse. Students design a data warehouse for a fictional organisation. Students should outline the Extract, Transform, Load (ETL) processes required to populate the data warehouse with relevant data, emphasising the importance of data quality and consistency.

Dashboard Design (Case study, 15%, Individual). To enhance business intelligence skills through designing a clear and insightful BI dashboard, emphasizing key performance indicators (KPIs) and ethical considerations in data processes and decision-making. Students to design a comprehensive BI dashboard for a given business scenario. Students should consider key performance indicators (KPIs) and design a dashboard that provides meaningful insights to decision-makers. The emphasis should be on clarity and simplicity in dashboard design, including ethical considerations of how data is collected, processed, and utilised in decision-making processes and practices for a business intelligence system.

BI Analysis and Implementation (Project, 40%, Group, group and individually assessed). Develop a business intelligence solution that adds value and competitive advantage. Students are to develop a business intelligence conceptual solution for a real-case scenario. Business Intelligence life cycle will be used as a roadmap to understand how data and information transform into intelligence, and how different applications/technologies can be used to analyse and report data. This assessment task is divided into two components. (1) Report and (2) Presentation. At least 10% of these components are marked individually and distributed in both the report and presentation, i.e., 40% (30% group, 10% individually).

By taking this subject, you will gain valuable skills in generating, sharing, retaining, and applying information and knowledge within corporations, which are crucial for enhancing business efficiency and decision-making processes.

These skills will not only help you become proficient in managing business processes but also make you an asset in any organisational setting that relies on data-driven decision-making.

Students work on group component (5%) and individual sections of their project (20%).

In this task, students are expected to demonstrate the main features of their data exploration prototype. All group members are expected to actively contribute to their prototype demo and will be asked on-the-spot questions about different features of the prototype, including brief statement of the problem, the underlying data structures, data quality and integration practices and visual ethics, multidimensional model and data exploration features. Students present group component (5%) and individual sections of their project (10%).

Visual data exploration prototype - report (Report, 30%, Group, group and individually assessed). Students develop capability in designing a visual data exploration prototype. Students work in groups to design multidimensional models suitable for non-technical stakeholders as well as implement a prototype using a commercial data visualisation software. Students report group component (5%) and individual sections of their project (25%).

Prototyping project reflection (Reflection, 20%, Individual). To reflect on the project in the form of key lessons learned. Following group presentations, each student reflects on the lessons learned from their own group project and the in-class presentations given by other groups. The reflection focuses on the central question: "If given an opportunity to do this project again, what would I do differently?" The reflection is expected to cover the whole life-cycle of the project, starting from the analysis of stakeholder problems, problem-driven (rather than data-driven) visual data exploration needs of different stakeholders, identification and ethical harvesting of relevant data, data quality, integration, data modeling for the identified stakeholders, design and implementation of a data exploration environment all the way to project presentations and lessons learned.

Taking the Information Systems (IS) perspective, rather than the more common Data Science or IT perspectives, this subject focuses on the latest developments and professional practices in data visualisation and visual analytics for non-technical decision-makers.

Recognising the importance of data visualisation literacy in various disciplines, including IS, this subject stands out by emphasising (i) understanding the reasons behind using data visualisation in addition to learning how to create them, (ii) identifying business and organisational cases along with their requirements, stakeholders, and problem space, (iii) visual ethics and the responsible use of visual data, and (iv) utilising commercial data visualisation software instead of elaborate coding.
In short, the subject aims for visual problem exploration "through data" rather than the creation of static visual outputs.
To achieve this, you will be taught through a combination of lectures and studios with a focus on design thinking exercises and ethical visual analytics.
You will develop the necessary skills and mindset for problem finding and solving through visual data exploration that goes beyond creating static visual outputs.

These skills include identifying different stakeholders and analysing their decision-making needs and environments, problem formulation, finding and ethically harvesting relevant data, ensuring data quality, data integration, multidimensional modelling, and developing a data exploration prototype using commercial data visualisation software.

Focusing on value creation and the decision-making needs of different stakeholders, you will also learn how to use data-driven visual storytelling and other contemporary techniques to explore the problem space, inform, influence, and inspire various types of stakeholders, including those in business and IT.

To demonstrate critical thinking and understanding of social, environmental and project management considerations in evaluating case studies of real engineering projects. Each student will individually assess an engineering project from the supplied case studies, considering project management, environmental, and societal aspects. Students will be expected to conduct extensive research on the selected project using reliable sources and to apply critical thinking skills. Students are required to submit an evaluation report, which will be assessed and the content will be used for Assessment Task 2.

Economic Project Appraisal: Critical Analysis (Written submission, 30%, Individual). To demonstrate the ability to evaluate the economic perspective in case studies of real engineering projects. Following Assessment Task 1, Students work individually to analyse and appraise an engineering project from the same case study through an economic lens. Students will be expected to conduct extensive research on the selected project using reliable sources and to apply critical thinking skills. The task submission includes a written report and an Excel file.

Holistic Project Review and Recommendations (Combination, 40%, Group, group and individually assessed). Demonstrate critical thinking by analysing and critiquing engineering reports from systems-thinking and ethical perspectives. In groups, students will critique a real-world case study of an engineering project, and report their findings in a written report (20%) and an oral presentation (20%). Assignment task 3A: Written report (20%): Students are required to submit a written report that critically evaluates the project, with a focus on analysing trade-offs between sustainability dimensions (social, environmental, and economic), ethical and professional responsibility considerations, and provide well-justified recommendations for improvement. -The written report will be moderated by SPARKPlus to give individual results for each student . Assignment task 3B: Presentation (20%): In-class task; students present their findings and respond to questions from the tutor and peers. All students are required to participate in preparing presentation materials and present their work. The presentation is 12 minutes, followed by 8-10 minutes of Q&A (total 20 minutes). - The mark breakdown for the presentation is 75% group work (15 marks) and 25% individual performance (5 marks).

Scoping Investigation: Project Context, Opportunities and Challenges (Written submission, 20%, Individual). This assessment requires students to investigate the project context to develop an evidence-based understanding of the factors that will influence the design of an engineering solution. Working individually within their project team, students analyse one aspect of the project context, including its opportunities, challenges, stakeholders and broader system environment. The analysis establishes the foundation for the engineering design work undertaken in Assessment 2, where individual investigations are synthesised into a collaborative design proposal and subsequently informs the detailed project developed in Assessment 3.

Interim Report and Presentation (Combination, 40%, Group, group and individually assessed). Report: Group assessed 20% Presentation: Individually assessed 20% This assessment builds directly on the project context investigations undertaken in Assessment 1. Student teams will consolidate the individual analyses completed by team members and use this evidence to develop and justify a preliminary sustainable engineering design proposal. Teams will investigate alternative engineering solutions, apply sustainability frameworks, undertake technical, environmental, social and economic analyses and use a structured multi-criteria decision-making approach to identify a preferred design solution. The assessment requires students to justify design decisions using evidence gathered in Assessment 1 and critically evaluate alternative solutions before progressing to the detailed engineering proposal developed in Assessment 3.

Final Report and Presentation (Combination, 40%, Group, group and individually assessed). Report: Group assessed 10% Presentation: Individually assessed 30% This assessment builds on the preliminary engineering proposal developed in Assessment 2. Student teams refine their proposed engineering solution by incorporating feedback received throughout the design process and developing a detailed final sustainable engineering proposal that addresses all requirements of the Request for Proposal (RfP). The assessment requires students to justify design decisions in different project phases through detailed sustainability analysis, while demonstrating systems thinking. Individually, students progressively demonstrate their understanding of the team's engineering proposal through the Engineering Design Reviews conducted during tutorial sessions in Weeks 10 and 11. The final client presentation in Week 12 requires each student to individually defend the team's engineering design by explaining and justifying key design decisions, technical analyses and sustainability considerations, while reflecting on how feedback, collaboration and iterative design informed the evolution of the final engineering solution and their professional capability development.

You must conduct a comprehensive analysis that demonstrates your ability to assess complex engineering proposals against the specified evaluation criteria. Your evaluation will require you to critically analyse each proposal's technical merit, project management approach, compliance with professional standards, and overall suitability for the project requirements. You will identify risks, assess value for money, and provide a justified recommendation with supporting evidence. This assessment develops your skills in interpreting technical documents, applying critical thinking to complex decisions, and communicating professional recommendations to stakeholders.

Contractor Response to RFT (Written submission, 35%, Group, individually assessed). This assessment challenges you to develop a comprehensive contractor response to a complex engineering RFT requiring multidisciplinary integration. Working in multidisciplinary teams (4-6 students), you will collaborate to create a professional RFT response document that directly addresses tender evaluation criteria, demonstrates technical capability, presents competitive commercial proposals, and meets professional procurement standards. This component is worth 35% and completed as a group. The groups mark is moderated by SPARKPlus and each student gets an individual mark.

Consortium Charter and Peer Review Portfolio (Creative project/portfolio/showcase, 10%, Individual). You will individually develop an assessment that demonstrates your personal accountability for analysing project information, applying relevant project management and engineering theory, and exercising professional judgement. This individual component focuses on integrating into a consortium, contributing to a shared charter, and providing structured peer feedback to partner firms to evaluate feasibility, identify key risks, and communicate a justified position aligned with client and project needs. Although the work takes place within a group, you are assessed individually. This component is worth 10% and completed individually.

Presentation Portfolio (Presentation, 35%, Group, group and individually assessed). You will build a presentation portfolio throughout the semester, demonstrating your professional communication skills across multiple contexts. Your portfolio consists of a final management presentation worth 30% by default, with opportunities to "lock in" up to one third of these marks (10%) through in-class presentation activities. When you participate in in-class presentations, those marks are secured early and reduce the weight of your final presentation accordingly. For example, if you earn 10% through in-class activities, your final presentation becomes worth 20% instead of 30%. This approach allows you to practice and build confidence while reducing the pressure on your final assessment. You can choose to do only the final presentation for the full 30%, or engage with in-class opportunities to distribute your marks across multiple lower-stakes presentations. The portfolio approach recognises that communication skills develop through practice and provides multiple opportunities to showcase your abilities in professional engineering contexts.

Use security tools to run cryptographic schemes and perform cryptographic analysis and attacks through eight labs throughout the session. Implementation project (Project, 50%, Group, group and individually assessed). Cryptographic specific project topics, such as implementing cryptographic algorithms, developing cryptographic attacks and configuring cryptographic systems, will be provided to students. A group of students (normally three) will be required to research appropriate practical techniques and carry out hands-on work to complete their chosen task. Students must also reflect on how these techniques are used more broadly in society to help individuals and organisations manage issues such as digital identity, security and information privacy. The assessment will cover group work and individual contribution. The group project will be assessed by tutors in-class based on the task completion and questions on the tasks. 40% project marks are for the group assessment and 60% project marks are for students' individual work. In this subject, you will delve into the critical role of cryptographic techniques in maintaining data confidentiality and ensuring data integrity.

Cybersecurity Capstone Portfolio (Portfolio, 100%, Individual). To document the iterative learning process and artefacts that demonstrate the achievement of learning goals related to cybersecurity. Students are expected to work in teams assuming the role of a professional colleague throughout the project phase. Although students work in teams, submissions are assessed individually. The Cybersecurity Capstone Portfolio is designed around a series of component parts. To meet the pass performance level of the portfolio, all components must be included. A performance level rubric is used to identify individual progress during the teaching session in view of students making individual improvements to their performance level based on continuous feedback and opportunities for personal reflection. The components of the portfolio include: Component 1: Individual Learning Contract Agreement Groupwork: Individual The intent of this component is to identify and document project direction, and set personal goals for the project duration. Each team member will create an Individual Learning Contract (ILC), and have it agreed to by their academic mentor(s). The ILC will be created in Canvas as an online assignment using a template provided. The ILC should describe activities that will enable each team member to gain additional knowledge and skills that will enhance the student's contribution to the team and product. Each team member is expected to select at least two technical and two non-technical learning activities, generally different than their peers. Component 2 Personal Design and Learning Journal Groupwork: Individual The intent of this component is to record and reflect on individual learning, design process, experiences and feedback received while working on the team product. Each student creates a Personal Design and Learning Journal (PDLJ) and records their learning, experiences and reflections on a regular basis. Students must keep their journal using a professional record-keeping tool as used in industry or research. The first purpose of the PDLJ is to document your individual contribution to the team product development by including evidence of work done and reflections on what worked, what didn't work and what you might do differently in future while working on the product development. The second purpose of the PDLJ is to document your progress against your own ILC goals set near the start of the session. You must curate evidence of your individual learning regularly throughout the session that demonstrates how you progressively achieve the goals articulated in the Individual Learning Contract (ILC). As well as receiving feedback from academic mentors, students may also be asked to share their progress with other students for peer feedback in some weeks. Participating in giving and receiving peer feedback, and reflecting on and documenting feedback, forms part of this task. Each team member must be able to demonstrate a history of regular contributions throughout the session. It is a requirement that the PDLJ be submitted at regular intervals. Feedback will be provided (either by staff or peers) for PDLJs submitted on time by the deadlines on Canvas. In the overall assessment, the PDLJ will be considered together with other artefacts in the portfolio in determining an individual's final grade according to the performance level rubric. Component 3: Team Product/Prototype Proposal and Pitch Groupwork: Group, group and individually assessed The intent of this component is to define the scope of the cybersecurity capstone project and to negotiate the scope and outcomes with the product owner and mentor. Project teams submit a written proposal for their product/prototype and have it agreed to by their product owner(s) and academic mentor(s). The proposal should include agreed deliverables and a timeline for the work to be carried out. The length of the proposal should be sufficient to fully describe the proposed Product, deliverables and timeline. A template with suggested section headings will be provided as guidance. This component is group assessed (all team members will include the same written proposal in their portfolio). Teams must also 'pitch' their product proposal in an oral presentation. All members of a team must participate in the pitch. This component is individually assessed. Component 4: Team Product/Prototype Delivery Groupwork: Group, group and individually assessed The intent of this component is to demonstrate your ability to deliver a cybersecurity capstone project to an agreed scope. In doing so, each team member also demonstrates their capacity to solve problems, create solutions, develop design specifications, implement the product/prototype, work in teams, communicate professionally and manage time and tasks. There are three sub-parts to this component: A presentation delivered in class (roadshow) that describes what was produced, including a demonstration where appropriate. The presentation is individually assessed. The product itself and a report and video that describes the product development process and outcomes. The size of the report will depend upon the complexity of the product and the number of students in the team. The video should be approximately 3 minutes, and the intended audience is your future employer. The report and video is group assessed (one submission per team), but individual grades may be moderated based on team member's overall contribution and evidence curated in their individual PDLJ. A communication log of meetings with the product owner, which clearly presents the meeting schedules, attendees and summary of discussions. This will typically be part of the final report. This part is also group assessed (one communication log per team), but individual grades may be moderated. All students must be present in class for the final presentation/demonstration, and all students must have contributed to the project throughout the session, including meetings with the product owner. The report should document the process followed, and contributions by individual team members.

Management of a technological innovation (Report, 45%, Individual). This assessment task helps students implement their knowledge of technology management activities and tools in a company context. The student should document a critical analysis of their organisation's current TM processes and practices/capabilities like an audit exercise. Then, the student will discuss how to implement a new technological innovation within the organisation. This task will allow students to see the link between technologies and TM activities. Adopting tools to analyse the implementation of technological innovation will facilitate students to observe the gaps in current TM practices. Then, the student will develop solutions to overcome the observed gaps. The student is encouraged to engage and interview their organization's executive leaders to make this a practice-based assignment. They will use materials presented to them from module-2 to module-4

Assessing potential implications of a new technology (Report, 25%, Individual). This task aims to guide students to research all potential impacts of new technology and develop a mitigation strategy to overcome any negative effects generated by this new technology. The student will be able to evaluate the impact of technological change by analysing and presenting the potential impact of technological change on stakeholders (such as employees, customers, and society) of an organisation. The analysis will cover both the positive and negative effects of technologies. Then, the student will focus on designing solutions to overcome any adverse effects of technological changes on personal, organizational, and societal levels.

text: Current state executive brief (Reflection, 15%, Individual). Business and industries are in different stages of theirs journeys towards a digital future and are facing a variety of challenges along the way. In times where digital technologies supercharge life cycles and competitive environments, it is important for business to stay on top. This assessment item focusses on an initial assessment of an organisation with respect to its digital progress. This assessment task therefore provides you with an opportunity to apply your understanding of these considerations to a specific case. Please consider a business of your choice. This could be the company you work for or another company of your choice (possibly in an industry you are passionate about and for which you have some background knowledge and some information that is publicly available). This will be the organisation you work with for all assessments. Be sure to look ahead at the other assessments before deciding on an organisation to work with. Some criteria for selecting your company: You need to be able to access information about your company's current digital strategy. The company's current digital strategy needs room for improvement. If they already have an innovative digital strategy they're probably not a good choice to work with for this subject. The company's executive members are considering a large investment program to prepare the business for a digital future. As a newly hired digital strategy consultant, you are asked to provide an assessment brief, summarising the current position of the company's digital journey. In this short executive report, they are expecting brief answers to the following questions: Q1: To what extent does your organisation currently rely on digital technology? Where on the evolution of the 4 industrial revolutions do you see your organisation? Q2: What could be the potential opportunities going forward based in the free perfect and instant characteristics of digital information goods? Q3: What could be the potential challenges for your business of choice? What have you learned from challenges or successes other companies have had?

text: Digital strategy pitch (Presentation, 45%, Individual). Everyone knows by now that digital processes are essential. They have now asked you to give them a pitch presentation, outlining key recommendations to a roadmap initiating successful and sustainable digital change. A use case for AI in business (Report, 15%, Individual). This assessment item focusses on the initial identification of a use case for AI in a business environment. Businesses are facing a variety of challenges in the digital age and AI can be a possible solution to tackle those challenges. This assessment task provides you with an opportunity to apply your understanding of these considerations to a specific case. Please consider a business of your choice. This could be the company you work for or another company of your choice (possibly in an industry you are passionate about and for which you have some background knowledge and some information that is publicly available). The company's executive members are considering a large investment program to prepare the business for a digital future. AI could become one important pillar of this program. As a first step, the executives have asked you to conduct an initial exploration of possible use cases for AI across the business. They are expecting a brief overview in the style of a management summary addressing the following questions: What are the key challenges that the company's industry is facing in the current competitive environment of rapid digital disruption? How does the company currently perform in relation to its main competitors? How could the power of AI be exploited to address those challenges?

Machine Learning Proof-of-Concept (Project, 45%, Individual). This assessment item evaluates your learning towards the data collection, feature engineering, design, evaluation, and execution of a data analytical model, providing appropriate context-based recommendations. In this assessment, you evaluate the listed skills in three main themes of machine learning techniques, namely, unsupervised learning, supervised learning, and learning by experience. Following on from the initial exploration of use cases, technical management is now advising you to develop a proof-of-concept for the application of machine learning models. For this, you are provided with a real-world dataset for the assessment. By using the course analytical software, you should analyse the data through your own analysis plan, compare the different ML techniques, and propose context-based recommendations. Also, you should respond to some questions using the output of the designed and executed analytical models. It requires you to understand and apply the techniques and skills covered in the subject. As a deliverable technical management is expecting a handbook outlining your model results and a report to describe and justify your results. You are provided with a real-world dataset for to be analysed using unsupervised learning techniques/clustering. Part A: Analysing data using Unsupervised learning techniques (20%) Part B: Analysing data using Supervised learning techniques (25%)

AI Roadmap (Presentation, 40%, Individual). This assessment task aims at consolidating previous findings into a compelling business proposal. It builds on the initial exploration in assessment task 1 and the technical modelling in assessment task 2 and puts those previous findings into the context of competitive advantage for the business in focus. You can reflect on specific business as well as wider societal impacts of AI and to develop their findings into a compelling narrative addressed at a senior business audience. After the successful development of the proof-of-concept, the company's technical executive is excited about the prospect of utilising AI to strengthen the company's technical capabilities. However, large investments require proper planning and due diligence, and AI is only one of several possible projects competing for the same funding. Therefore, the executive is asking you to prepare an AI roadmap presentation for their technical review board headed by the CTO to make a case for an AI implementation project to get approval. They expect a 20-minute video presentation covering the following aspects (your slides should support the narrative flow of your argument): Description of selected use case for AI Which challenges are you aiming to address? Which features of AI are you proposing to use? Justification of use case and alignment with business strategy Why is the proposed project the best use of company resources? How will it contribute to strengthen to company's competitive positioning? Reflection on impact What are limitations and challenges you expect along the way and how can they be addressed? What are the socio-cultural and ethical impacts of the proposed project? How are cultural and historical contexts and privacy relevant to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders' data reflected in the projects ethical, social and economic impacts? Expected benefits and ways to measure success Which benefits and advantages do you expect from successful implementation? Which metrics and KPIs do you propose to measure ongoing success? Project plan What are the key work packages, milestones and deliverables? What is the rough timeline for implementation? Who are the key stakeholders (technical and non-technical) that need to be involved? In addition, the management has asked you to prepare a management summary as a take home document after the pitch presentation. This summary should provide a concise yet comprehensive summary of your argument following the typical structure of a management summary (subject matter, methods, findings, conclusions, recommendations, limitations).

Journal Assignment (Journal, 20%, Individual). To develop students' sensitivities and perceptions about how people use technology in their everyday activities and the ability to articulate various issues around the design and use of technology from the perspective of its usability and usefulness. Students will work individually to produce three journal entries describing and critiquing real-world digital systems in terms of their design and use, that are relevant to the interests of the subject. While students are provided with the actual digital systems they have to write about for entries #1 and #2, they will have to actively seek out their own example for entry #3. For these journal entries, students have to observe and document people's interactions with the systems as well as apply their understanding of various design/usability concepts, theories and principles to analyse and critique the experience people have during these interactions. These may include poorly designed systems that do not support the activity they are used for, as well as systems that work well within their situation of use. Ongoing and formative feedback on journal entries #1 and #2 will support students to produce good work. A more detailed assessment brief for each journal entry will be provided on Canvas.

Project proposal, plan, and methodology (Presentation, 20%, Group, group and individually assessed). This task allows students to master their skills of searching and evaluating the existing methods and solutions, understanding and exploring the context of existing approaches, and synthesizing this knowledge to inform industrial project. This task also develops skills in preparing and writing project proposal, selecting appropriate methodology and preparing feasible plan of work. Find an industrial partner with which the project will be done. Meet with the industry mentors and discuss the topic for the project. Based on the discussions with the mentors formulate problem and prepare project proposal (including research questions and objectives). Prepare appropriate project plan that will enable you to effectively manage work in the group. Make sure that clear work breakdown structure is created, tasks are assigned to individuals and adequate amount of time is allocated to each task. Workloads should be designed in a way that each team member does similar amount of work. Propose appropriate methodology to answer stated objectives and solve the proposed problem. Prepare the presentation that clearly outline all above points. Students individually will be required to work on the presentation and then meet and agree on one presentation. Evidence of their individual work will be appendix to this presentation.

Report of project proposals (Report, 20%, Individual). This task allows students to further improve their critical analysis skills and ability to prepare proper peer review. Students will be asked to review presentation about project proposal prepared by other group. For a given project proposal a critical analysis that will clearly state advantages and shortcomings of reviewed proposal needs to be prepared. This will be done in a form of structured report.

Research paper (Report, 30%, Group, group and individually assessed). This task allows students to improve their skills in conducting and evaluating real-world projects. This task also develops skills in preparing and writing reports. Review your project proposal (Assessment Task 1) in the context of the feedback you have received from Task 1 and from your mentors and peer-reviews. Include in your report revised list of project goals and objectives (maximum word count: 1,000 words per review). Design of experiment - prepare detailed plan of your experiments or investigation; what and how will be done. Make sure that the designed experiments will help you to fulfil the stated goals from Assessment Task 1 (maximum word count: 1,000 words per review). Conduct the experiment and present your results analysis - you need to prepare and conduct your planned experiments. The results you obtain need to be presented in a way that is easy to understand and that they help you, later on, with your discussion. Presented analysis should provide answer to the project goal presented in your project proposal (Assessment Task 1) (maximum word count: 1,000 words per review). Verify and validate of research outcomes - you need to assess the validity of your results. Make sure that what you present is significant and correct (maximum word count: 500 words per review). Discussion and conclusions - you are expected to discuss and summarise your study. Also identify the potential future directions for your study (maximum word count: 500 words per review). Students individually will be required to work on the verification and validation of research outcomes, discussion and conclusions and then meet and agree on final version they submit. Evidence of their individual work will be appendix to this report.

Reflection and portfolio (Portfolio, 30%, Individual). This task allows students to improve their skills in reflection on their process of teamwork and self-management. This task also develops skills in managing team artefacts. Regularly reflect on what you set out to achieve in your weekly project work, how you approached each task, what problems were encountered, what could be done differently, and what you learnt from the experience. Use the artefacts produced through the process of completing each task to examine group processes you are using, and evaluate the progress of the project. Demonstrate how theory or research informs your practice and show the evolution of work-in-progress and associated peer feedback on work and issues presented by others. In class, time within each workshop will be devoted to monitoring the progress of each group. Therefore, each class member will be required to contribute to a weekly group presentation or retrospective meeting: showing a project deliverable they have developed or are in the process of developing, discussing the process of development, and inviting input and constructive feedback from other class members. Many different forms of contribution to your group's project, and reflection on your process can be assembled into this reflective journal and portfolio. Examples include, sketches and plans, lists, evidence of git commits, ticket completions, code reviews, research findings, results analysis scripts. Within your reflection, one method to structure your reflections is to use the following format: Recount - describe an event that happened within your projects progress React - describe how this made you react/feel (annoyed, pleased, frustrated, disappointed etc.). Analyse - work out why this event caused this reaction. Improve - describe how to either ensure that this is repeated (if the reaction was positive) or how to avoid or minimise the impact of this event occurring in future (if the reaction was negative).

A use case for AI in business (Report, 15%, Individual). This assessment item focusses on the initial identification of a use case for AI in a business environment. Businesses are facing a variety of challenges in the digital age and AI can be a possible solution to tackle those challenges. This assessment task provides you with an opportunity to apply your understanding of these considerations to a specific case. Please consider a business of your choice. This could be the company you work for or another company of your choice (possibly in an industry you are passionate about and for which you have some background knowledge and some information that is publicly available). The company's executive members are considering a large investment program to prepare the business for a digital future. AI could become one important pillar of this program. As a first step, the executives have asked you to conduct an initial exploration of possible use cases for AI across the business. They are expecting a brief overview in the style of a management summary addressing the following questions: What are the key challenges that the company's industry is facing in the current competitive environment of rapid digital disruption? How does the company currently perform in relation to its main competitors? How could the power of AI be exploited to address those challenges?

Machine Learning Proof-of-Concept (Project, 45%, Individual). This assessment item evaluates your learning towards the data collection, feature engineering, design, evaluation, and execution of a data analytical model, providing appropriate context-based recommendations. In this assessment, you evaluate the listed skills in three main themes of machine learning techniques, namely, unsupervised learning, supervised learning, and learning by experience. Following on from the initial exploration of use cases, technical management is now advising you to develop a proof-of-concept for the application of machine learning models. For this, you are provided with a real-world dataset for the assessment. By using the course analytical software, you should analyse the data through your own analysis plan, compare the different ML techniques, and propose context-based recommendations. Also, you should respond to some questions using the output of the designed and executed analytical models. It requires you to understand and apply the techniques and skills covered in the subject. As a deliverable technical management is expecting a handbook outlining your model results and a report to describe and justify your results. You are provided with a real-world dataset for to be analysed using unsupervised learning techniques/clustering. Part A: Analysing data using Unsupervised learning techniques (20%) Part B: Analysing data using Supervised learning techniques (25%)

AI Roadmap (Presentation, 40%, Individual). This assessment task aims at consolidating previous findings into a compelling business proposal. It builds on the initial exploration in assessment task 1 and the technical modelling in assessment task 2 and puts those previous findings into the context of competitive advantage for the business in focus. You can reflect on specific business as well as wider societal impacts of AI and to develop their findings into a compelling narrative addressed at a senior business audience. After the successful development of the proof-of-concept, the company's technical executive is excited about the prospect of utilising AI to strengthen the company's technical capabilities. However, large investments require proper planning and due diligence, and AI is only one of several possible projects competing for the same funding. Therefore, the executive is asking you to prepare an AI roadmap presentation for their technical review board headed by the CTO to make a case for an AI implementation project to get approval. They expect a 10-minute live presentation and 5-minute Q&A covering the following aspects (your slides should support the narrative flow of your argument): Description of selected use case for AI Which challenges are you aiming to address? Which features of AI are you proposing to use? Justification of use case and alignment with business strategy Why is the proposed project the best use of company resources? How will it contribute to strengthen to company's competitive positioning? Reflection on impact What are limitations and challenges you expect along the way and how can they be addressed? What are the socio-cultural and ethical impacts of the proposed project? Expected benefits and ways to measure success Which benefits and advantages do you expect from successful implementation? Which metrics and KPIs do you propose to measure ongoing success? Project plan What are the key work packages, milestones and deliverables? What is the rough timeline for implementation? Who are the key stakeholders (technical and non-technical) that need to be involved? In addition, the management has asked you to prepare a management summary as a take home document after the pitch presentation. This summary should provide a concise yet comprehensive summary of your argument following the typical structure of a management summary (subject matter, methods, findings, conclusions, recommendations, limitations).

Cybersecurity Challenge Studio Portfolio (Creative project/portfolio/showcase, 100%). This subject is assessed through a single Portfolio. The purpose of this assessment is to document the full challenge process, evidence, and outcomes of the selected stream, and to present a professional, evidence-based account of what was completed, how the work was validated or evaluated, and what the scope, assumptions, and limitations are. Students must select one stream in Weeks 1 - 2 (Industry stream or Research stream), and the Portfolio requirements are aligned to the selected stream. The Portfolio must be professionally written and include step-by-step evidence, analysis, and reflection. Students must provide professional evidence of their work, such as screenshots, logs, experimental outputs, code, records of progress, and other relevant artefacts. Screenshots and other submitted evidence must include the student's identification details (for example, student ID/number) where required by the subject instructions. The Portfolio also includes a recorded presentation and demonstration that communicates the problem, approach, key technical steps, evidence of outcomes, and limitations in a manner suitable for a professional audience. Assessment requirements differ by stream, as follows. Industry stream Students in the Industry stream complete a practice-to-project portfolio structured through four milestones. Milestone A: Learning contract completion and Hands-on training selection and execution In Weeks 1 - 2, students select a set of hands-on training tasks based on the signed learning contract. Tasks carry different point values based on difficulty and may be subject to selection limits for lower-difficulty tasks. Students must construct a task combination that meets the training requirement. The Portfolio must document the key steps, technical process, evidence, and analysis of the completed work. A progress check is due in Week 5. Milestone B: Student-designed project development Students develop a project derived from their selected training direction and apply appropriate security standards and/or methods to support security-by-design and validation. A complete project and Portfolio draft is due in Week 10. Milestone C: Cross-group penetration testing and professional testing documentation Each group is paired with another group, with both groups testing each other's systems or solutions through security testing activities such as penetration testing, and producing professional testing documentation. This documentation must include scope, approach, evidence, findings, and recommendations. Evidence from Milestones A - C must be consolidated into the final Portfolio. This is not a competitive milestone; students' performance will be evaluated on the quality and professionalism of their testing documentation. This milestone is due in Week 12. Milestone D: Recorded presentation and demonstration Students submit a recorded presentation and demonstration. The presentation must clearly communicate the challenge, approach, key technical steps, evidence of outcomes, and limitations in a manner suitable for a professional audience. The presentation should also propose potential ways to address the limitations identified in Milestone C. This milestone is due in Week 14. Research stream Students in the Research stream complete a research-to-evidence portfolio structured through four milestones. Milestone A: Learning contract completion, paper selection, method analysis, and implementation/replication with comparative experiments In Weeks 1 - 2, students select a target paper based on the signed learning contract, either provided by staff or sourced from appropriate venues. Students then analyse the research background, motivation, feasibility, and assumptions of the selected work, and implement or replicate the proposed method(s). Comparative experiments must be conducted against relevant baselines or related methods, including evaluation across different datasets or settings where appropriate. A progress check is due in Week 5. Milestone B: Limitations analysis and improvement proposal Students identify limitations of the selected work and propose a justified improvement or extension. Where feasible, the proposal should be supported by evidence such as additional experiments, ablation studies, or a clear analytical or mathematical derivation. A complete Portfolio draft is due in Week 10. Milestone C: Cross-group peer analysis Each group is paired with another group to conduct reciprocal peer analysis of each other's work. Students critique and analyse the other group's work to identify weaknesses, limitations, and the research-to-practice gap. Where appropriate, groups may apply alternative datasets or settings and/or different adversarial models or attack strategies to evaluate usability and security properties. Findings from this milestone must be incorporated into the final Portfolio. This milestone is due in Week 12. Milestone D: Recorded presentation and demonstration Students submit a recorded presentation and demonstration. The presentation must clearly communicate the research problem, approach, key technical steps, evidence of outcomes, and limitations in a manner suitable for a professional audience. The presentation should also propose potential ways to address the limitations identified in Milestone C. This milestone is due in Week 14.

Weekly exercises (Exercises, 40%, Individual). To demonstrate programming knowledge and ability by designing and implementing small programs or adapting existing programs. For each exercise the student will be presented with sections of code, and instructions for alterations they are required to make to the code to achieve some specific goal. It prepares you for the commercial world by developing your understanding of different roles within an enterprise through a business planning framework.

Desktop study (Report plus presentation, 25%, Group, individually assessed). To develop skills in finding, evaluating and referencing information relevant to the team project and to develop understanding of the Indigenous Australian context of the project. In this task, students will work with their team to identify areas for investigation then individually investigate and evaluate information to become familiar with the context of their group project, critically evaluating information and sources to synthesise their research into a clear and concise written summary. Students will write a summary of the research that they have conducted so far, ensuring that information sources found and used are reliable and relevant, and are referenced correctly in their summary using APA 7th Edition referencing style. As part of the process of developing the desktop study, you will present a mindmap in class showing your chosen Design Area, the specific focus of your desktop study and the information that needs to be researched. This process will assist in confirming appropriate direction and improving the desktop study prior to its submission. Students will be assessed on both the desktop study itself and the documentation of the processes taken to produce it. Task A: Mindmap presentation: 5% Task B: Desktop study: 20%

Design presentation (Presentation, 45%, Group, individually assessed). This core subject exposes you to ideas regarding the scope of what engineering actually is, considerations regarding engineering in the Australian context, and the broad impacts engineering decisions have on people, community and the environment.

Through authentic engineering experiences you will build your professional skills and knowledge, providing a solid foundation for your continuous professional development journey as a future engineer.

The subject is centred around completing the Engineers Without Borders Challenge for which you will work in a team to develop engineering solutions to local real-world challenges on behalf of a partner Australian Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander Community Organisation.

You will form a team with peers and working together in and outside class you will research and refine the problem and design considerations, ideate and prototype potential solutions that will work in the community context, and ultimately propose a fully developed design idea that would benefit the partner community.

In completing the challenge you will develop your professional interdisciplinary skills such as research skills, learn and apply the engineering design process, develop an understanding of and consider socio-technical issues, build your professional communications skills in engineering contexts, and learn to lead and participate in team processes.

Computer modelling, analysis, and steel design of the proposed building. (Report, 0%, Group, individually assessed). To utilise computer modelling and analysis tools to design and optimise a steel structure for the proposed building. This task involves creating a comprehensive model of the building, performing structural analysis, and designing the steel components to meet the specified requirements. Teams are to prepare a preliminary (draft) written report as per the criterion outlined in the Project Brief and specifications grading rubric made available on the brief project release (for students to gauge their performance level). There are 2 parts for submission. Part 1: Addressing feedback based on questions raised during Oral presentation Project briefs Part 2: Conceptual design report incorporating the feedback containing Building Description General Overview: Provide a brief description of the building, including its purpose, size, and any unique architectural features. Structural System: Outline the chosen structural system for the building (e.g., moment-resisting frames, braced frames, etc.). Site Information Location: Details about the building site, including geographic location, soil conditions, and any relevant environmental considerations. Design Loads: Specify the loads considered in the design, including dead loads, live loads, wind loads, seismic loads, and any other relevant loads based on local codes and standards. Computer Modelling Software Used: List and briefly describe the software tools employed for modelling and analysis. Modelling Approach: Explain the process of creating the model, including: Geometry definition Material properties Load application Boundary conditions and support Structural Analysis Analysis Types: Describe the types of analyses performed (e.g., static analysis, dynamic analysis, buckling analysis). Results Interpretation: Present and interpret the results of the analysis, including: Displacement profiles Internal force distributions Stress and strain distributions Critical Sections: Identify and discuss critical sections and elements in the structure. Steel Design Design Codes and Standards: Specify the design codes and standards followed (e.g., AS 4100 for steel structures). Member Design: Detail the design process for the steel members, including: Selection of steel sections Calculation of capacities (bending, shear, axial) Check against design criteria (strength, stability, serviceability) Connection Design: Outline the design of connections, covering: Bolted and welded connections Connection detailing Verification of connection capacities Optimisation Design Iterations: Discuss the iterative process used to optimise the design for efficiency and cost-effectiveness. Alternative Solutions: Present any alternative design solutions considered and the rationale for the final design choice. Sustainability Considerations Material Efficiency: Discuss strategies for minimising material use without compromising structural integrity. Environmental Impact: Evaluate the environmental impact of the chosen design and materials. Lifecycle Analysis: Provide an overview of the lifecycle analysis for the steel structure

Team members will be delivering a formal oral presentation on the final design project. Criteria outlined in the final design presentation specifications grading rubric is made available on the brief project release (for students to gauge their performance level). Subgroup B will deliver presentations and address feedback from the client brief report. Subgroup A will answer the questions at the end of presentation. Presentation should include: Drawing Types General Arrangement Drawings : Show the overall layout and major components of the steel structure. Detail Drawings : Provide detailed views of specific elements, such as connections and joints. Section Drawings : Illustrate cross-sectional views to highlight internal features. b. Standards and Conventions Drawing Standards : Follow industry standards for steel design drawings (e.g., AS 1100). Notation and Symbols : Use appropriate symbols and notations for clarity and consistency. c. Key Components Member Details : Dimensions and specifications of beams, columns, and other steel members. Connection Details : Specifications for bolted and welded connections, including materials and fastening methods. Fabrication Notes : Instructions for fabrication, including cutting, welding, and assembly processes. d. Communication Techniques Clarity and Precision : Ensure drawings are clear, precise, and free of ambiguities. Annotations : Include comprehensive annotations to explain design decisions and details. Revisions and Updates : Document any revisions and updates to drawings to maintain accuracy. Presentation Delivery Format : Present drawings in both digital and hard copy formats. Review and Feedback : Conduct review sessions with stakeholders to gather feedback and make necessary adjustments.

Final Design Project Portfolio (Portfolio, 100%, Group, individually assessed). To document and reflect on the design process of steel and timber. The final submission is made up of all the artefacts as well as the feedback, interpretation and actioning of feedback that were submitted during the session. A key element will be the reflection on the current design practices and where or what areas students will want to focus on going forward. The portfolio should include a cover page, table of contents, and an introduction outlining its purpose. Each artefact should be presented with the original submission, feedback received, and the revised version, along with a reflection on how the feedback was actioned and a claim to the grade. The final section should focus on a comprehensive reflection where students discuss their current design practices and identify areas for future improvement. This structure ensures that the portfolio not only showcases the work but also highlights the student's engagement with feedback and ongoing professional development.

This Pre-Professional design studio introduces you to practical techniques in design of steel and timber structures.

The emphasis is on analysis and design of structural members and connections of steel and timber structures, computer-aided structural design and design optimisation techniques, and producing construction sketches for the main structural components of buildings.
This subject is based on authentic professional projects relevant to the building industry that you may wish to enter, providing material for a portfolio after graduation.
You will work with a wide range of data inputs to apply innovative and thoughtful opportunities to learn critical review of engineering documents/projects and disciplinary research skills.
This Steel and Timber Design Studio enables you to demonstrate achievement of professional skills by working on real-world projects.
Facilitated by a mixture of studio facilitators, academic experts, and industry partners, you will work in teams to define problems, and identify, develop, and implement solutions.
Using a design-thinking framework and systems thinking, you will regularly engage in pitching and critiquing work among peers.

In the assessments, you are required to demonstrate your achievement of each of the subject learning objectives using a collection of artefacts and reflections that meet the standard performance criteria for each grade.

Analyse and evaluate the relationships between active, public and private transport users, different forms of transport infrastructure, vehicles and different transport modes in planning for a sustainable transport system. (B.1)
Apply the basic terminology, empirical data analysis and modelling concepts of transport planning and traffic engineering practice to effectively manage transport systems. (D.1)
Examine the interaction between land-use development, transport infrastructure supply and demand as well as overall traffic operations to develop transport management plans for the community. (C.1)

Photo Travel Diary of a Journey (Project, 15%, Individual). To assess a student's ability to complete a set of divergent thinking activities fundamental to transport planning, by focusing on defining transport systems and relationships, and analysing the impact of operations and behaviour on the performance of these systems. Students are required to complete an individual photo diary report of a trip undertaken by public transport, private transport or active transport that highlights three critical operational characteristics important to transport users (customers). Students will be provided with a PowerPoint template in which to present their photos and short descriptions. Online submission made through Canvas

Transport Planning Evaluation Report (Report, 35%, Individual). To evaluate a student's ability to apply the theoretical concepts of traffic engineering and develop solutions to real-world operational problems within a transport network (focused on public transport). Students are required to generate an evaluation and recommendations report related to a case study of a real-world transport planning problem. The case study will focus on a comparison between different transport modes. Students will need to assess the transport and land use impacts to define and design potential solutions. Students will be required to submit a report responding to the brief provided. Online submission made through Canvas.

Transport Operations Technical Report (Report, 15%, Individual). To evaluate and apply the fundamental aspects of transport engineering with a particular focus on traffic engineering and modelling. Students solve a local traffic problem reflecting the design and decision-making methodologies used by a traffic engineers in practice. Students will undertake a data analysis exercise which assesses the conceptual understanding of the material covered in Weeks 7 to 9 of the subject. Students will be required to process traffic data related to a local problem and conduct further analysis to provide recommendations and a solution to the problem. Online submission made through Canvas.

Transport Modelling and Operations Report (Report, 35%, Individual). To evaluate and apply the theoretical concepts of traffic engineering and develop solutions to real-world operational problems within a road network. Students are required to complete a report that is related to the subject content delivered in Weeks 7 to 11. The project will involve students applying the 4-step planning process to evaluate the current and future transport conditions of a specified study area. Students will be assessed on their ability to apply the fundamental components of traffic flow theory and transport modelling. In addition, upon evaluating conditions, students will be required to develop traffic management solutions to alleviate issues identified through data analysis and additional contextual information related to the study area. Students will need to present the modelling methodology, results and traffic management solutions in a report format, similar to what is expected in professional settings and will be assessed on technical accuracy and clarity in presentation. Online submission made through Canvas.

This introductory subject explores transport engineering within civil and environmental engineering, emphasising sustainable design and planning.
It encompasses transport planning, focusing on public transport systems analysis, design, and evaluation.
In addition, you'll learn the basics of traffic engineering, where you will develop a '4-step transport model' to assess regional travel demands, crucial for infrastructure feasibility and design.
You'll also grasp traffic flow theory fundamentals, enabling you to evaluate transport capacity and infrastructure.
Practical case studies, including local area traffic management schemes, illustrate applications of theory, equipping you with relevant assessment tools and skills to be a transport professional.

Required topics quiz (Quiz/test, 20%, Individual). This assessment task encourages students to engage and learn the subject progressively. To engage in tutorial discussions effectively students need to demonstrate their understanding of the topic by answering a quiz on the relevant topic. Watch the lecture, complete the quiz. Lectures and related material are provided online so that students can study the material at a time that suits them. A quiz is provided for each topic to enable students to check their progress toward mastering the topic.

Elective topic quiz (Quiz/test, 15%, Individual). This assessment task encourages students to study, understand and apply the means of developing specialised software architectures. There are four specialised software architectures suited to particular problems. Choose any two of them, study them, then answer their respective quizzes.

Team project (Project, 45%, Group, group and individually assessed). Work in a team to develop an architecture for a specific system in a given context. The project is a group assignment to be completed in small teams. You are expected to develop a software architecture for a non-trivial system using the techniques learned in this subject.

Peer review (Laboratory/practical, 20%, Group, individually assessed). Develop and practice the professional skill of reviewing and critiquing the work of peers. Each group will present their work in progress to another group for their review and critique. Reviews are completed using a review form (currently Google forms) and submitted on completion. Peer reviews are conducted in the tutorial room.
