Quiz (Quiz/test, 10%, Individual). The quiz consists of a small number (10 - 20) of multiple choice questions. The quiz will explore the extent of your knowledge and understanding across the weekly topics. The questions will be taken from: * The Lecture slides and Readings for weeks 1 - 6. * The Labs for Lectures 1 - 6. To answer the questions correctly you need to understand the question topic. To do this you will need to attend the weekly lecture/discussion sessions, perform the weekly lab and discuss the lab questions with your group and read the weekly readings. There will be a quiz Q&A document released two weeks before the quiz. There will be a practice quiz a week before the quiz.

Assignment (Project, 30%, Group, group and individually assessed). The assignment is designed for students to demonstrate their skill in researching digital forensic topics in a real world environment. Students will practice their skills in collecting evidence from a digital device for later analysis by a forensic specialist. This assessment is a review of a Forensics topic of current interest and aims to add knowledge to the material provided in class. The topic is chosen from a list provided. Students need to research the topic online, download and explore some apps/tools and prepare a report and short presentation. Students need to provide detail in depth so that others can replicate the work. Students need to submit a Proposal to confirm the assignment topic and plan in the middle of the semester. By the end of the semester, students need to submit a Report and give a Presentation. There will be a proposal guide and report guide in the assignment introduction. Feedback will be provided via Canvas.

Skills tests (Demonstration, 40%, Individual). Skills Based Assessments (SBAs) are designed for students to demonstrate their skill in locating forensic evidence on a digital device. Students are given an image file acquired from a suspect's laptop and asked to assess if allegations of failing to comply with company policies regarding the use of company time or intellectual property are proven. Topics are taken from the weekly labs.

Weekly skills test (Laboratory/practical, 20%, Group, individually assessed). For students to demonstrate mastery of weekly lab concepts. Students are given a small assignment to complete in each week's lab class. Students can complete the assignment in class or in their own time. There will be 10 weekly tasks, each worth 2%. Students upload their answers for tutor feedback prior to the next lab class.
This subject aims to develop an in-depth understanding of digital forensics principles as well as the tools and configurations available. The following topics are covered:
The Legal Process in forensic investigation. Digital Evidence. Australian Privacy Principles
Duties of First Responders
Data Acquisition from Hard Disks and Networks
Disk file systems including FAT32 and NTFS
Windows Registry analysis
Linux Artifacts of forensic interest
Metadata in Graphics, Documents and Camera images The following tools are covered:
Protocol sniffers/analyzers
TCP/IP utilities
Windows Internals utilities
Hard Disk (HDD) utilities
Web-based resources The predominant lab types are procedural, skills integration challenges, troubleshooting, and model building
Upon completion of the subject, students will be able to perform the following tasks:
Describe the security threats facing modern network infrastructures
Secure network device access
Implement forensic analysis on network devices
Implement forensic analysis on hard disk devices
Administer effective security policies
Collect forensics material for specialist analysis
In this practice-based subject, you will engage in laboratory-based learning to determine if a crime has been committed through the acquisition, analysis, and reporting of digital evidence.

Your studies will focus on forensic analysis of network data, including the recovery of website visitation evidence relevant for court cases, alongside scrutinising digital storage devices to identify and retrieve critical data.

You will also delve into the examination of operating systems to unearth hidden data, perform detailed analysis of metadata to gain deeper insights, and apply rigorous forensic principles to produce sound and defensible reports.
Through these hands-on activities, you will develop a comprehensive understanding of digital forensics and its applications in real-world scenarios.
Analyse, design and implement a programmable digital system based on a user requirement specification, and investigate advanced digital systems architectures. (C.1)
Demonstrate in-depth understanding of the analysis/design and implementation of advanced digital hardware at medium scale computer system building block level. (C.1)

Utilise computer-aided design, including the use of VHDL or Verilog specification, simulation and programmable FPGA implementation technologies, Register transfer level, Data path and control units. (D.1)

Learning Contract (Project, 10%, Individual). To create a plan i.e. a learning contract, to develop a prototype digital device using an FPGA. Develop a learning contract for this course using the following process: 1. Decide on project; 2. Create specifications for the deliverable; 3. Create a timeline for the work needed; 4. Document potential risks and how these might be dealt with; 5. Document materials and intellectual property (IP) needed for the proposed work. Throughout the first few weeks of class we will be looking at aspects of the learning contract.

Mid-project presentation and report (Project, 30%, Individual). To provide a progress update and gain feedback on project progress. Students will prepare a presentation and accompanying report on the progress of their project against the goals and plan in their learning contract. 20% of the marks are for the presentation and 10% for the report. Criteria for the presentation and report will be published online.

Final project report and presentation (Project, 60%, Individual). To present final prototype, demonstrate use and deliver report on project. Students must deliver a presentation and submit an accompanying report outlining the outcomes of your project paying particular attention to what was agreed in the learning contract. A demonstration of the developed prototype must also be provided during the presentation and documented in the report. 40% of the marks are for the report and 20% are for the presentation. Criteria for the report and presentation will be published online.
Advanced digital design through the development of a prototype design agreed upon in the student's learning contract. Learning components encompassed by this include: 1. Verilog/VHDL programming
2. Revision of digital design concepts: combinatorial design, sequential design, state machines, arithmetic logic units
3. Digital design architectures
4. Timing and interfacing requirements
This studio delves into the analysis, design, and implementation of an advanced computing node, focusing on digital hardware at the medium-scale system level.

It builds upon introductory digital systems knowledge, employing studio-based learning that covers the digital design process, functional design, implementation technologies, advanced digital architectures, and memory and I/O systems within project work.
Post completion, you'll be adept at planning, designing, and developing digital intellectual property (IP) using FPGAs and hardware description languages (HDLs) such as Verilog and VHDL.

Evaluate modular components such as microcontrollers, sensors and actuators using datasheets to inform technology choices. (D.1)

Individual learning contract (Portfolio, 30%, Individual). To provide an opportunity for guided self-learning of topics related to embedded systems. At the start of the teaching session, students create an individual learning contract (ILC) and then have it agreed to by their academic mentor(s). The ILC should describe a series of activities that will enable the student to gain knowledge and skills in the area of embedded systems, particularly to enhance the student's contribution to the team and the product to be developed. Students generally complete this individual learning independently and outside of class time, and check in regularly with their academic mentor to update progress, receive feedback and identify any challenges encountered. Assessment of the ILC will take place in three phases: ILC setup and agreement at the start of session ILC maintenance and monitoring during the session ILC finalisation at the end of session Students document their individual learning in a portfolio.

Embedded systems project (Portfolio, 50%, Group, individually assessed). To demonstrate the ability to design, implement, test and evaluate a product based around an embedded system. Students work in teams to design and implement an embedded systems product. Each group must prepare a portfolio documenting their contributions, design decisions and insights relating to the product throughout the teaching session. Weekly updates are expected, with each update building on and extending the previous work in the portfolio. By the final submission at the end of session, the portfolio should be a complete record of the work undertaken. Students must submit their portfolio for assessment and feedback a minimum of 5 times during the session, but may submit up to a maximum of 10 times. The individual mark of each student will be determined based on the individual contribution to the group submissions.

Final report (Report, 20%, Group, group and individually assessed). To demonstrate professional written and oral communication skills in documenting and describing an embedded systems product. Teams of students prepare and present a final report describing the product that was implemented. The report should describe design choices, technology choices, and the implementation and testing strategy. A separate section should provide an evaluation of the product, to identify benefits and limitations of the approach chosen, what you learned along the way and what you might do differently in a future embedded systems design. As a team, students also need to deliver a short presentation of their implemented product to their peers and teaching staff. The presentation is to include technical aspects of the product design as well as a reflection on how collaboration as a team impacted on the quality of the product. All team members should contribute to the presentation. The audience for both of these deliverables is industry professional engineers.

Skills Based Assessment (Laboratory/practical, 30%, Individual). Apply a complex array of environmental and planning legislation, and law cases to the field of civil and environmental engineering contexts. (B.1)
Analyse the balance between the development and the environment, then derive strategies to resolve conflicts in the interaction between development and environmental protection. (B.1)
Describe and apply technical, legal and social considerations in the planning process. (B.1)

Environmental law & planning scenario analysis (Report, 30%, Individual). This assessment task aims to assist students to consolidate and refine their ability to analyse environmental and planning legislation. This assessment task consists of two interlinked components: Task 1a Environmental Law (worth 15% of total assessment value) and Task 1b Environmental Planning (worth 15% of total assessment value). In Task 1a, students will select and critically analyse an environmental law case or dispute involving development planning. A suggested list will be made available to students online on Canvas. When writing this report and presentation, students are encouraged to draw similarities and adapt approaches from precedent cases or court decisions as reported in literature. They will demonstrate understanding and ability to apply environmental law to a specific and simple case. In Task 1b, students will be required to conduct risk-cost-benefit analysis of a proposed development plan and write a report. A suggested list will also be made available to students online on Canvas. They will identify relevant environmental and planning legislation and policies, interpret their meanings, objectives, and implications with respect to the proposed land use or development. They will also demonstrate and interpret the inter-connection between planning and environmental law, and propose solutions to relevant planning problems.

Environmental planning case analysis report & presentation (Report, 40%, Individual). In this assessment task students will develop problem solving, critical analysis and communication skills to resolve conflicts between development and environmental conservation and apply these skills in the planning process. In this assessment task (worth 40% of total assessment value), students will present a written report and a verbal presentation to discuss the relevant environmental legislation and propose strategies to resolve legal conflicts. Students will be presented with a hypothetical scenario relating to an actual location or environmental law case in Australia. This assessment task consists of 2 stages (stage 1 and stage 2). In stage 1 (worth 5% of total assessment value), students are required to submit an outline of their case report. Students will receive feedback prior to the final submission of their case report. In stage 2, students are required to submit their case report (worth 25% of total assessment value) and a pre-recorded presentation (worth 10% of total assessment value).

Online quiz (Quiz/test, 30%, Individual). In this assessment task students will interpret the implication of contemporary environmental law in the context of land use and development planning. The online quiz will be open book. Students will apply their skills developed from the subject to gather information for environmental planning, interpret the meaning and implication of environmental law, assess the interaction between environmental law and other law discipline, and evaluate the impact of emerging issues and new technologies on the evolution of environmental law. These will be demonstrated through a series of short answer and multiple choice questions. This assessment will cover subject content in Blocks 1 to 4.

Environmental Law: The evolution of Environmental Law, the legal framework in Australia, environmental movement, the model environmental law, interaction between environmental law and development planning, and various legislations governing environmental planning with a focus on the NSW legal system including Protection of the Environment Operations Act, Waste Minimisation Act, the Independent Pricing and Regulatory Tribunal Act, the Sydney Water Corporatisation Act, and selected court decisions relating to pollution and land use issues. 2

Environmental Planning: Evolution of human settlement, Urban planning and sustainability, Neighbourhood planning concepts, planning approval pathway, case studies of the Sydney Olympic Park and the Greater Sydney Region Plan
This subject introduces you to key concepts and principles of environmental law to protect human health, biodiversity, and the environment in the context of resource management and land use planning.
You will explore the evolution of environmental legislation and regulations and their role in development planning and resource management, particularly in NSW.

You will also gain an understanding of NSW planning legislation, the planning process, and land use constraints, enhancing your ability to navigate legal, social, and environmental challenges in engineering projects.
The subject also aims to improve your communication skills in legal contexts and provide a conceptual and technical grasp of environmental planning and law.

You'll engage with topics like biodiversity conservation and the operation of the Environment Protection Authority, major environmental acts, and court decisions on development applications and pollution control.

Through tutorials and case studies, you will discuss contemporary environmental law cases, culminating in a discussion paper on an engineering-related environmental issue, preparing you to collaborate effectively with legal professionals.
Identify cognitive biases and heuristics that influence decision-making processes and mitigate their impact in various scenarios. (B.1)
Apply decision analysis tools and frameworks to evaluate and resolve complex problems. (C.1)

Implement diverse decision-making models, including model-driven, cognition-driven, and data-driven approaches, grasping their strengths, weaknesses, and optimal applications in real-world contexts. (D.1)
Utilise group and strategic decision-making strategies to solve complex decision situations across varied scenarios and organisational levels. (E.1)

Decision Diagnosis and Bias Analysis (Written submission, 20%, Individual). Students will select a real-world case study from a credible source and apply judgment and decision-making frameworks to analyse three key decision-making situations. They will identify the cognitive biases and heuristics influencing each decision, evaluate their impact on the decision-making process and outcomes, and recommend practical, evidence-based mitigation strategies. In addition to the written analysis, students are required to submit supporting appendices, including a Bias Identification Table, a Source Evaluation Table, an AI Use Declaration, and an Academic Integrity Statement, to demonstrate their analytical reasoning, critical evaluation of evidence, and responsible academic practice.

Designing Decision Support Systems (Written submission, 40%, Individual). This assessment develops students' ability to design, justify and evaluate decision support systems for complex real-world problems. Building on Assessment 1, students will critically evaluate the decision-making situations identified within their case study and determine which two decision situations would benefit most from structured decision support. For each selected situation, they will justify the most appropriate decision support approach, develop and apply the selected approach, interpret its outputs and critically evaluate its effectiveness. Unlike Assessment 1, which focused on understanding how cognitive biases influence decision making, this assessment focuses on designing decision support solutions that improve the quality of human judgement.

Group Decision-Making Report and Presentation (Combination, 40%, Group, group and individually assessed). Report: Group assessed 30% Presentation: Individually assessed 10% Report: This assessment builds directly on the work completed in Assessments 1 and 2. Student teams will select one case study from those previously analysed by group members and collaboratively develop an integrated organisational decision-making strategy for the selected case. Drawing on the cognitive bias analysis and decision support approaches developed in the earlier assessments, teams will synthesise and extend this work by applying group, strategic, leadership and agile decision-making frameworks to address a critical organisational decision problem. Teams will justify the integration of cognition-driven, model-driven and data-driven approaches, critically evaluate their effectiveness and develop evidence-based recommendations that reflect professional decision-making practice. Presentation: Students should demonstrate an individual understanding of the approaches used and explain their own contribution to the group's analysis.
Mindful judgment and ethical decision making
The psychology of judgment and decision making
Models of decision making (descriptive, statistical, and optimization models will be covered)
Heuristics and biases
The social side of judgment and decision making
Data-driven and AI-assisted decision making
This subject explores key theories and concepts in judgment and decision making, including biases, heuristics, and decision analysis, particularly under uncertainty.
You'll learn about decision-making models ranging from cognition-driven to model-driven and data-driven approaches, crucial for modern complex systems.
The subject also covers organisational principles for group, strategic, and leadership decision makings, enabling you to understand and apply effective decision-making strategies in various contexts.

Individual Charter (extended) (Report, 20%, Individual). Students are expected to prepare an extended project charter on a provided template. Further details of the project specifics will be available on canvas by week 2.

Group Project (Project, 70%, Group, group and individually assessed). Students will work in groups of up to six people to develop a detailed project management plan of an engineering project. (individual mark: 50 marks) Further details of the project specifics will be available on canvas by week 2.

Reflections (Report, 10%, Individual). Each student will submit an individual critical reflection report. The report will include student's self-assessment and evaluation of their learning and performance in the subject.

Project Identification and Context Analysis (Written submission, 35%, Individual). Students will individually identify a significant public engineering or infrastructure project from publicly available sources and prepare a concise analysis of the project. The analysis will examine the project's objectives, purpose, and expected beneficiaries; describe its technical characteristics and implementation; and analyse the broader social, economic, political, and environmental context in which the project operates. Students will also consider the opportunities and constraints that may affect the project's successful implementation. This assessment provides the foundation for the comprehensive financial and economic evaluation undertaken in Assignment 2.

Project Financial and Economic Evaluation (Project, 30%, Group, group assessed). Following the investigations undertaken in Assignment 1, students will form groups and select one engineering or infrastructure project for comprehensive evaluation. Working collaboratively, they will undertake a comprehensive financial and economic (socio-economic) evaluation of the selected project. Using publicly available data and appropriate evaluation techniques, students will identify, classify, quantify, and assess project costs and benefits; undertake financial and economic cost-benefit analyses; calculate key viability indicators; evaluate project risks and uncertainties; and provide evidence-based recommendations regarding the project's financial and economic viability. The assessment requires students to integrate engineering, financial, economic, social, and environmental considerations to support informed investment decision-making. Individual marks may be adjusted based on peer evaluation using SPARKplus to reflect each student's contribution to the group work.

Executive Investment Pitch (Interactive oral, 35%, Individual). Building on the group work completed in Assignment 2, each student will individually deliver a 3-minute Executive Investment Pitch to a simulated decision-making panel, followed by a 2-minute interactive question-and-answer session. Students will communicate the outcomes of the project's financial and economic evaluation succinctly and persuasively to a non-technical audience. The pitch should clearly justify the recommended investment decision, demonstrating why the selected project is viable from financial, economic, social, and environmental perspectives. During the question-and-answer session, students will defend their recommendation, justify the underlying analysis and assumptions, and demonstrate their individual understanding of the group's financial and economic evaluation. The interactive oral assessment will be conducted during Week 12. As this is an individual assessment, attendance is mandatory, and students are expected to attend their allocated tutorial.

Topic and Case Study Analysis (Report, 20%, Individual). For students to predict and avoid failures due to human factors, design flaws, materials failure and extreme conditions. Students study the topics provided and select one based on their interest and background. Then, they identify and describe two engineering failures related to their topic that occurred previously. For each case study, students set the boundaries, identify stakeholders, define the inherent risk, describe the causal chain, and explore if the case studies affected or were affected by Indigenous communities.

Risk Management Plan (Report, 30%, Group, group assessed). For students to apply risk management principles and processes conforming with AS ISO 31000: 2018 in a case study Students prepare a risk management plan in accordance with AS ISO 31000: 2018 for one of the case studies investigated in assessment 1. Students need to: Define the system boundaries carefully; Establish the context clearly in accordance with the standard; Clearly state the risk tolerability criteria employed; Show evidence of consideration of alternatives for risk management; Include a discussion; and Consider aspects beyond the texts and subject materials.

Quantitative Risk Assessment and Decision Making (Report, 50%, Individual). For students to research their topic, assess, evaluate, and treat risks using quantitative risk assessment and risk-based decision-making techniques in a case study. This assessment is authentic and requires students to apply what they have learned and higher level thinking to solve complex problems in a similar way that they would do in professional practice. Students study their topic to understand the elements and parameters involved. They learn and apply appropriate quantitative techniques to conduct a risk assessment to verify the magnitude of the risk exposure in terms of deaths/injuries/damages/costs in one of the case studies prepared in assessment 1. Then, they explore different risk treatment options and select the best option(s) considering the time, cost, quality and scope constraints using a risk-based decision-making technique.

Group activities and project (Project, 50%, Group, group and individually assessed). Students will be required to join one of 6 groups each of which is divided into 5 teams of 5-6 students each. The aim of the groups is to come up with a sustainability initiative and high-level execution plan for UTS to implement within a 1 to 2-year period. The details of the project, group dynamics, conditions, requirements and constraints can be found in the detailed project description available through Canvas. Case study analysis (Exercises, 25%, Group, group and individually assessed). Each week students will be given a short video or text dealing with some aspect of leadership and responsibility. During the tutorial time, each team will analyse the material provided and answer a set of questions. On alternate weeks, each team will be required to either report to the rest of the cohort in a class discussion or to the teaching team in the form of a one-page written report due by the end of the day.

Weekly reflection and posting on discussion board (Reflection, 15%, Individual). Each student will be required to identify 2 persons they consider leaders from their own perspective - at least one of the chosen leaders must be a person that all the rest of the class either already knows or has the possibility of knowing about, e.g. Gandhi, while the other one can be a person in that student's life, only known to them. The task is to analyse the leadership of those persons from the perspective of each of the weekly topics discussed during the lectures and tutorials. The deliverable for this assessment is a weekly online posting of maximum 250 words on the discussion board of each team, which will be discussed and peer marked.

Weekly journal (Journal, 10%, Individual). Students will be required to peruse reputable media coverage of issues/problems affecting either domestic or international contexts and find an example of 'good' leadership and an example of 'bad' leadership. Students must explain what makes each case either 'good' or 'bad' leadership. The deliverable for this assessment is two submissions, each with 3 weekly 1-page (maximum) reports which will be peer marked and discussed during tutorials.

Online Problem Sets (Quiz/test, 30%, Individual). Group Assignment (Report, 20%, Group, group assessed). Students are required to prepare a financial model for a particular firm in order to analyse the current and future performance using various models and techniques. This assignment is based on collaborative work among group members for the creation of a financial model for your business. Your group is required to produce a financial model (using the guidelines available in Canvas) of your business. No complaints about group operation will be considered after the assignment has been submitted. Please see the assignment section of Canvas for full details.

Online Video Presentation (Presentation, 40%, Group, group and individually assessed). Students have to present the analysis and valuation of their case study in the seminar in order to draw conclusions about the feasibility of expansion/ replacement investment. Review Quizzes (Quiz/test, 15%, Individual). Regular quizzes are held each block to give students feedback on the progress in understanding key concepts and procedures. A 60 minute online quiz will be held on the dates and times specified in the Program.

Laboratory Test (Laboratory/practical, 25%, Individual). Lab activities allow students to link theory and practice using industry standard tools and techniques. Students will capture packets using the 'wireshark' software, and analyse the composition, flow and timing of packets and frames in a very similar way to what a professional telecommunication engineer would do in configuring and troubleshooting a real-world network. In the lab exam, students will demonstrate their capabilities to analyse traffic, identify faults and measure network performance in a simulated network environment. Students will retrieve an obfuscated Mininet lab exam script via Git, which they will execute in their virtual machine image. Using this script, you will need to complete a series of tasks on the emulated network, including (but not limited to) traffic analysis, route analysis, port scans, and various types of performance testing. Performance metrics may include measurements such as latency, jitter, packet loss and throughput. You will be expected to describe exactly how you performed each test that you used and provide a technically accurate interpretation of the results. The task will be a restricted open-book exam.

Final Exam (Examination, 40%, Individual). This provides an opportunity for students to demonstrate their individual understanding of key concepts and procedures as would be used in an industrial setting The final exam will be conducted in the form of supervised online exam for onshore students; offshore / remote students will be assessed via an oral exam/interview to be conducted via Zoom.

You will receive the highest mark exceeding 80%; if you fail to reach the 80% threshold by the third attempt, you will receive a mark of zero for this task.

Assessment Task 1 - Quality Planning and Analysis Report (Written submission, 35%, Individual). Students are required to prepare an individual written report on a topic related to Quality Planning and Analysis , selected from a list provided by the teaching team. The report should demonstrate a critical understanding of the selected topic by integrating relevant quality management concepts, contemporary research, and practical industry perspectives. The report should include the following components: Introduction and Problem Context - Introduce the selected topic and explain its significance. Literature Review - Critically synthesise the relevant literature using at least 5 high-quality academic references . Analysis and Discussion - Apply and discuss appropriate quality planning and analysis tools and techniques relevant to the selected topic. Current Challenges and Improvement Opportunities - Identify key challenges, gaps, and opportunities for quality improvement. Conclusion and Recommendations - Summarise the key findings and provide practical recommendations. The report should demonstrate evidence-based analysis, and effective academic writing, supported by appropriate referencing throughout.

Assessment Task 2 - Quality Planning and Analysis Group Project (Combination, 30%, Group, group assessed). This assessment is designed to provide students with an opportunity to apply the quality planning and analysis concepts, tools, and techniques covered throughout the subject to a practical, real-world scenario. Working collaboratively, students will analyse a product, service, or work system and develop a structured quality improvement approach using appropriate quality management methodologies. As the focus of your project, the group may choose one of the following options: Design and production of a product (e.g., household appliances, electronic devices, clothing and footwear, transportation equipment, etc.); Design and delivery of a service (e.g., healthcare, education, hospitality, tourism, logistics, etc.); or Design and execution of a work or project (e.g., construction of a house, bridge, road, or other engineering works). Throughout the project, students are expected to apply appropriate quality planning and analysis tools, where relevant, such as DMAIC, Kano Analysis, Quality Function Deployment (QFD), Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA), Cost of Quality (CoQ), Design for Quality (DfQ), Statistical Process Control (SPC), Lean Manufacturing, and other continuous improvement techniques covered in the subject. The assessment comprises two components: Group Report (20%) Weighting: 20% Submission: One report per group Length: Approximately 5,000 words (excluding references and appendices) The report should demonstrate the systematic application of quality planning and analysis tools to investigate the selected case, identify quality-related issues, evaluate findings, and develop practical recommendations supported by appropriate evidence. Group Presentation (10%) Weighting: 10% Duration: 6~7 minutes per group. The presentation should clearly communicate the project objectives, analytical approach, key findings, recommendations, and practical implications. All group members are expected to contribute to the presentation and demonstrate an understanding of the project.

Assessment Task 3 - Quality Improvement Solution (Combination, 35%, Individual). This assessment provides students with an opportunity to individually investigate and present how quality planning and analysis principles are applied within their discipline or a selected industry sector. Students may choose a topic related to manufacturing, construction, computer science, logistics, healthcare, or another relevant field, and critically examine how quality management contributes to improving organisational performance, product or service quality, process efficiency, customer satisfaction, and continuous improvement. Students are expected to demonstrate the application of appropriate quality planning and analysis concepts, tools, and methodologies discussed throughout the subject, such as Six Sigma, DMAIC, Kano Analysis, Quality Function Deployment (QFD), Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA), Cost of Quality (CoQ), Design for Quality (DfQ), Statistical Process Control (SPC), and Lean Manufacturing, where relevant to the selected topic. The assessment comprises two components: 1. Individual Presentation (20%) - Each student will deliver an individual presentation of up to 6~7 minutes . The presentation should communicate the student's analysis in a clear, logical, and professional manner and include the following: Introduction and Industry Context - Introduce the selected product, service, or work system and explain its industry relevance. Application of Quality Planning and Analysis Concepts - Demonstrate the application of relevant quality planning and analysis tools, techniques, and engineering principles to investigate the selected case. Key Challenges and Improvement Opportunities - Critically discuss the major quality-related challenges identified and propose practical improvement opportunities supported by appropriate analysis. Conclusions and Practical Implications - Summarise the key findings, present evidence-based recommendations, and discuss their implications for engineering and industry practice. 2. Individual Written Submission (15%) - Students will submit an individual technical report of approximately 2000 words (excluding references and appendices) that supports their presentation. The report should clearly describe the engineering problem, present the quality planning and analysis methods and tools applied, interpret the findings, and critically discuss their practical implications and limitations.

Communicating Concepts in Data Ethics (Essay, 50%, Individual). Concept map and article Part 1 Concept Map/Visual Representation Students will draw on concepts covered in Module 1 to produce a concept map/visual representation (with ~250 words of text) that describes the complexity of an ethical issue of their choice (e.g. it might be: concerns about privacy, discrimination or fairness when behavioural data from computer-equipped cars is shared insurance companies; crime statistics and behavioural data being used in ways that result in the over-policing of volunerable and marginalised populations; data from streaming services and its relation to media production and tastemaking; personal health data and privacy etc). The concept map/visual representation should show an understanding of the exact type of data and processes involed in the situation (Week 1). It should also include a clear statement of the stakes (e.g. why should we be concerned about this?) and make reference to, or compare, at least two of the ethical theories covered in Module 1 such as social contract theory, utilitarianism, virtue ethics, kantian ethics, deontology and consequentialism (Week 2). Part 2 Article/Think Piece Drawing on feedback from Part 1, students will write a short article explaining the ethical problem outlined in Part 1 in simple terms understood by a general audience. Students should use a real world example or a hypothetical to illustrate key points and expand on key ideas from the concept map/ visual representation by conducting their own desk research. The revised concept map/ visual representation should appear in the article/think piece as a figure with figure legend and a clear connection to the article's narrative. All sources used and referred to must be appropriately referenced either in APA style and/or with hyperlinks. A list of references must also be provided. In text references and the reference list does not count towards the word limit for this task. Further details are provided on the subject's Canvas site. Examples of previous work will be provided.

Response to Hypothetical Scenario (Case study, 50%, Individual). Students select a case from a range of provided hypothetical scenarios involving data malpractice in different industries (e.g. banking, healthcare, policiing etc) to work on. Each case asks students to assume a stakholder identity and write a response from that particualr point of view. Information on the style and format of the response varies for each of the cases and information will be provided at the end of Week 4. Students will formulate a response to the hypotehtical scenario that includes: a) situating the case within an appropriate legal and regulatory context (i.e. showing they understand what laws and regulations apply) and a clear articulation of data types and processes involved in the scenario. b) an interpretation of actual or potential forms of malpractice inherent in the case expressed through an appropriate code of ethics along with a discussion of the strengths and weaknesses of exisiting codes of ethics. c) a set of recommendations for better day to day practice and/or the potential reform of data-related policy, regulation and law. A list of references must also be provided. In text references and the reference list does not count towards the word limit for this task. Further details are provided on the subject's Canvas site. Examples of previous work will be provided.
Module 1: Key concepts
In the first module students are introduced to key concepts and definitions across the two main areas of the subject
Module one covers two key questions: (1) What is data, why is it valuable and how is “datafication” related to processes that turn data into information, knowledge and economic value

This part of the module encourages students to build a more nuanced understanding of what different types of data there are, what different forms they can take and what they can and can’t do for organisations, institutions, society and individuals
(2) What ethical precepts guide the way we might think about good data stewardship?

Here students are introduced to some simple interpretations of different Western ethical traditions (utilitarianism, social contract, deontology) and make sense of them in light of current data-driven practices, problems and opportunities
This insight is then used to interpret and unpack various ethical and regulatory frameworks covered in the second module
Module 2: Frameworks
In the second module, students are introduced to a number of legal and regulatory frameworks that govern contemporary data stewardship practice

The second module casts a wide net across the regulatory landscape covering areas including consumer rights, health, geospatial data standards, intellectual property and licencing of datasets, metadata/quality standards, Freedom of Information (FOI), open data and the data sovereignty of indigenous and minority groups
Students also examine the role of different regulatory bodies and the channels of recourse available to both consumers and institutions when there are instances of data harms or malpractice
Module 3: Case Studies
In the third module, students are presented with a list of case studies from which they can choose and explore areas/industries/problems based on their own interests
This provides a more individualised way of consolidating learnings from modules one and two

The subject is designed to provide students from a range of disciplines and backgrounds with a fundamental understanding of the Australian legal system, the Common Law traditions underpinning it and its operation within the Australian federal structure and the Westminster system.

Its objective is for students to develop an understanding of the Australian legal framework and the role of law and then consider the law in a business context in regulating individual and commercial relationships.
This provides a basis for undertaking further studies in law in Australia.
An overall introduction to the subject is provided in the 'Get Started' Module.
The subject topics are then structured in eleven Modules numbered 1-11.

The Modules comprise topics which address learning about the Australian legal system and the civil, criminal and business relationships it regulates, and several topics covering public international law.
Modules 1-3 introduce students to the Australian legal system and help them understand the operation of Australian law.

These topics aim to equip students with a foundational understanding of the operation of the Australian legal system to enable an effective transition into the more specialised learning involved with Modules 4-9.
Modules 10-11 explore international law with some reflection on the relationship of Australian law to international law.
Module 12 enables students to revise the main topics for exam preparation.

Mock Trial (Moot) (Project, 40%). The Moot will require students to form into pairs. Three student pairs will be involved in each Moot. These student pairs will play different roles (and perform different work). The first pair will act as the legal representatives of an employee, or a group of employees (the Employee's Representatives). They will be required to: Prepare written submissions (2,000 words) one week in advance of the scheduled Moot. In these submissions, the Employee's Representatives will need to address the legal and factual issues relevant to their client's position; and Present their client's case in a mock trial to be conducted in class (for 7 minutes each); and Answer questions posed by the Judges in the mock trial. The second student pair will act as the legal representatives of the employer (the Employer's Representatives). They will be required to: Prepare written submissions (2,000 words) one week in advance of the scheduled Moot. In these submissions, the Employer's Representatives will need to address the legal and factual issues relevant to their client's position; and Present their client's case in a mock trial to be conducted in class (for 7 minutes each); and Answer questions posed by the Judges in the mock trial. The third student pair will act as the adjudicators (the Judges). They will be required to: Prepare questions for the Employer's Representatives and Employee's Representatives in advance of the Moot (after reviewing the written submissions of each of these representatives); Ask questions to test and critically evaluate the submissions of the parties Representatives in the mock trial; and, Within one week of the mock trial, draft a decision and appropriate orders in which the legal and factual issues of the case are analysed and resolved (2,000 words). Half of each student's mark for the assessment will be based on the written submissions (in the case of the Employer's and Employee's Representatives) and the written decision in the case of the Judges. This mark will be shared by each student pair. The other half of each student's mark for the assessment will be based upon that student's presentation in the mock trial.

Collaborative Presentation (Presentation, 30%). This is a group task, and it is intended that each student in the group will receive the same mark as other students in the group. However, individual marks may be adjusted: if group members do not respond in a timely way to communication from other group members or their teacher; or if there is clear evidence that a group member is contributing significantly more or less to the written and oral tasks: For example, during the presentation, one group member answers all of the questions asked by other students or the tutorial leader, or one group member does not speak during the presentation. The groups will comprise 5 students per group (depending on the number of students in the class) and students will self-allocate into groups from the first week. An announcement will be made via CANVAS that will enable students to self-allocate into groups using a link that will be provided. So that students can earn marks, it is important that students self-allocate into a group in the tutorial from their timetable. I.e. If your tutorial is Monday 11am you must present in the Monday 11am group. Your teachers will be monitoring the groups, any student who allocates outside of their own tutorial will be automatically reallocated to a group in the correct tutorial. Apart from online tutorial groups, students must present in-person. If students do not attend their presentation for any foreseeable reason including due to personal, study, work and travel commitments, you will receive zero for your presentation. If you miss an in-person assessment, due to illness or misadventure, you need to apply for special consideration.. Each group will also be required to submit an online written submission explaining their answers, with a maximum of 1,000 words - it is an outline only, not a script - due one week before their presentation. For example if your presentation is on Monday Week 3 your written answer must be submitted by Monday Week 2. A penalty of 5% per day will apply for every day the written submission is late - this includes weekends. This will allow your teacher to provide feedback which you can incorporate into your work. If you receive 6.5/10 or fewer marks for the written component, you may resubmit via the submission portal available from Canvas. However, the maximum marks you can earn on a resubmission are 7/10. Students are not permitted to use Artificial Intelligence for the written component of the presentation and any evidence that students have used Artificial Intelligence for the written component will be grounds for an allegation of student misconduct. All presentation materials (i.e. the final presentation) must be submitted to your teacher (tutor) by Friday before the presentation. For example if your presentation is on Monday Week 3 your presentation materials must be submitted by Friday Week 2 . A penalty of 5% per day will apply for every day the presentation material is late - this includes weekends Additional information on the formal requirements of the oral presentation is available on Canvas under "Assignments" and "Assessment Task 1 - Collaborative Presentation" Written component: The written component should not be more than a maximum of 1,000 words in length (anything exceeding this limit will not be marked). Oral presentation: The presentation by each group is to be a maximum of 25 minutes plus discussion time. Students must factor into this time, questions from other students and the tutor. An indicative guide should be 25 minutes for presentation and 10 minutes for any questions and discussion (=35 minutes in total). More comprehensive information on the formal requirements of the oral presentation is available on Canvas in the 'Collaborative Presentation' folder. I f students exceed the 25 minutes for any reason and are unable to present ALL students will receive an average of the highest presenting mark and zero. Students are permitted to use Artificial Intelligence for the oral presentation, but only to enable them to develop their slides and presentation materials. Self- and Peer Assessment: After the presentation, students must log into SparkPLUS on Canvas to self-assess and assess the contribution of each student involved in the assessment against a set of defined criteria and give feedback in the comments section. SparkPLUS will be available after the census date. Tutorial Participation: It is important to attend all of your scheduled tutorials, not just the one when your group is presenting. There is an 80% attendance requirement, failure to meet this may result in the student being requested to attend a VIVA following the final take home exam, and/or a W or F grade pending further academic investigation.

Early and Mid In-class Multiple Choice Quiz (Quiz/test, 20%). Students will complete two in class quizzes - each quiz is 15 minutes long with 10 questions and each quiz is worth 10 marks. The quizzes will be CLOSED book and invigilated by the tutor. For online classes, students must keep their cameras on for the entire duration of the quiz and microphone/camera for the peer assessment/review at the end of the formal quiz. For face to face students, students will swap papers and undergo peer assessment/review at the end of the formal quiz. Students are not permitted to use Artificial Intelligence in the two quizzes. Students MUST sit the quiz in their own scheduled class. Exceptions to this will only be made in extenuating circumstances. OTHERWISE the student must make it up with special consideration approval during the final assessment period. Please see the tutorial programme for dates of quizzes and the topics to be examined in each quiz. The two quizzes will examine Topic 2 "Incorporation and Characteristics of a Company", Topic 4 "Inside the Company - Rules, Members and Directors"., Topic 5 "ASIC, Fundraising and Disclosure", and Topic 3 "Company's liability in crime, contract and CSR". For Topic 3, please concentrate on agency. Extensions for Mid-session Quiz/Special consideration etc. must be made using the Faculty's 'Request for an Extension' Form. Please see https://www.uts.edu.au/current-students/current-students-information-faculty-law/assessment. The following are not adequate grounds for an extension: Assessment in other subjects being due at the same time. Work and travel commitments. Social and family commitments (weddings engagements, birthdays etc) If you miss your quiz, any make-up quiz (subject to approval of special consideration) will be during the final assessment period in that session. To assist students in their preparation for this assignment, there are practice quizzes of 10-15 questions available on Canvas in each Module. Practising the weekly online practice quizzes encourages students to undertake formative self-assessment of their progress throughout the session on their understanding of the principles of Applied Company Law. Undertaking the practice quizzes will: Give students immediate feedback on whether they have properly understood the topics discussed in lectures and text books; Reinforce the knowledge learned in lectures and readings; and Prepare students on what to expect as part of the mid-session exam. Early identification of problem areas enables the student to undertake further study or seek further assistance from their tutor or through online discussion or collaboration with their peers to ensure that they properly understand principles before the final exam. Students will receive immediate feedback upon completion of each practice quiz.

Final Exam (individual) (Final exam, 50%). The final examination is the culmination of the subject where students demonstrate their understanding and mastery of it. The purpose of the end - of-session examination is to test students' legal knowledge of Applied Company Law, legal problem solving and written communication skills. As indicated above, the exam will be invigilated by Proctor U and will be two hours long (no additional reading time), with a word limit of 2,500 words. Further information on the final examination will be provided closer to the examination period by way of an announcement on Canvas. The exam will be of two hours' duration and is a limited open book exam. More details about the materials and resources you may refer to, will be available from CANVAS. Also please keep in mind that students are not permitted to use Artificial Intelligence in any way to assist in answering exam questions. In addition, no communication between students and other people will be permitted during the exam, and any evidence of copying, plagiarism or the use of Artificial Intelligence will be grounds for an allegation of student misconduct. The final exam will focus primarily on Directors and Directors' Duties, Members' Remedies, Companies in Difficulties and External Administration, as well as Reports: Accounts and Audit. The questions, however, assume knowledge you have already studied - for example, the company as a separate legal entity. Assessments will not be accepted after the due date and time, unless extenuating circumstances apply. Please note: Students are required to check their emails and be available throughout the entire exam period including Alternative exam period. Accommodations for the Main Exams and Alternative Exams will not be made for students who knowingly book holidays or other work or any such commitments during this time - other than for unforeseen circumstances, such as illness or misadventure. Also note: Students will have five business days to respond to a subject coordinator request to attend a VIVA or any matter related to their exam. This can occur either before exam results or after exam results in response to a request for review or otherwise. Failure to check emails and miss the VIVA will result in any of the following, a Fail Mark or a W Mark or a referral to the relevant Law Academic Officer - without further notification to the student. "I did not check my emails / I was overseas on holidays etc." is not a sufficient excuse.

Designing an experimental plan (Literature review, 30%, Individual). In biology, every sample is different. Plant cells are different from bacterial cells which are different again from mammalian cells. When trying to perform proteomics on these samples, each has to be treated in different ways. In addition, the analysis techniques used in proteomics generate different types of overlapping data. In this assessment, you will choose a sample and describe how you would best analyse the proteome of that sample to gain understanding of how proteoform abundance changes lead to changes in biology. In the process of producing an appropriate workflow, you learn about different proteomic techniques and what kind of data they produce. For you to gain an understanding of the principal concepts of proteomics and how the techniques and technology can be applied, you choose a specific topic related to your work or interests or be provided with a topic. Potential topics should be pitched to teaching staff for discussion, refinement and approval. After extensive reading of the current published literature, you will design a workflow that would produce the most comprehensive and useful dataset, referencing the relevant literature. The methodology MUST be tailored for the specific problem, NOT a list of generic methods, and use the most up to date techniques and instrumentation available. The workflow should consider the following (which is not an exhaustive list and can be extended): Sample preparation and extraction methods most appropriate for the sample and intention of the study. Proteoform or peptide fractionation methods. Analysis (mass spectrometry) methods. Potential bioinformatic analysis methods. The most important criteria is that you must show a critical analysis of what your proposed method can do and what it can't do (analyse proteoforms?) and describe alternatives that would make up for that short coming.

You will be asked to complete a number of tasks prior to and during your attendance in class. The most prevalent form of scientific communication is the peer-reviewed journal article and you will present your results in the form of a manuscript ready for publication, thus learning the important skills of data interpretation and presentation. You will write a short technical report in a form consistent with proteomic journals covering the techniques, results and interpretation of your proteomics experiment in the practical classes. The discussion must include critical analysis of your ability to perform the experiments correctly. The report should be in the format of a short communication to a journal; divided into Introduction, Materials and Methods, Results, Discussion and Conclusions.

The term "proteomics" can essentially be applied to any work on proteins, whether that work involves completely cataloguing the expressed proteome of a cell, characterising the post-translational modifications of proteoforms at the single molecule or whole proteome level, or the characterisation of proteoform-proteoform interactions and proteoform complexes, to name but a brief few

With this in mind, the objective of the practical component of this subject is to give an overview and introduction to the most common techniques used to extract, fractionate, analyse and quantitate the proteome of a cell

Interculturality in the Hood (Report, 40%, Individual). Spaces of intercultural encounters are found everywhere around us and are the building blocks of daily local encounters. The aim of this assignment is for you to research, engage with, and map interculturality in your neighbourhood as a local space of intercultural encounters, connections and diversity. You will create a presentation or report that introduces intercultural spaces in your neighbourhood and then engage with intercultural encounters in this area and reflect on your relation and positionality to them. This will include large and small cultural, contested, Indigenous, multicultural and hybrid spaces. You are to prepare a deliver a recorded video presentation describing and discussing a neighbourhood you are familiar with and that features five spaces which in some way signal or identify interculturality, including Indigenous and contested spaces. You should explain why these places are significant for intercultural encounters and how you personally connect to, or are positioned within, these spaces. You will justify the choice of specific spaces of intercultural encounters that also locate yourself in that setting. The task requires a critical examination of the interactions within each chosen place/space, relating them to intercultural concepts discussed in the lecture series. You should critically reflect on the complexity of intercultural encounters in each space and link them to intercultural concepts learnt about in this subject. This assignment encourages you to engage deeply with your local environment, offering a personal and analytical perspective on intercultural connections and the spaces that foster them. In addition to the subject and further readings, you should refer to at least two references that focus on your Hood/suburb or neighbourhood and that provide historical information about its cultural and demographic makeup.

The subject starts by giving you an overview of intercultural communication theories and how they are used to categorise and describe cultures

Critically reflecting on these theories, you will explore the notions of culture and identity in particular focussing on how these notions are shaped by communication and represented in our globalised world
Building on this foundation, you'll explore the complexities of cultural competence, including how cultural awareness is built
This is developed through critical reflection of case studies and your own intercultural encounters and experiences

You will have opportunities to explore different facets of intercultural life in Australia according to your particular area of professional interest and to apply the theoretical knowledge you have built to develop nuanced intercultural understandings
This subject introduces you the core concepts and debates in the interdisciplinary field of intercultural communication.
You'll be prepared for the interpersonal and dynamic nature of working in increasingly globalised workplaces and intercultural environments.
You'll use a problem-based approach to critically examine numerous frameworks and theories that allow you to interpret intercultural encounters in praxis-based scenarios.
You'll apply specific intercultural communication strategies and approaches for their relevance to industry, communities, workplaces and society more broadly.
